how_to_use: The 8 marks split evenly: about 4 questions from Labour and Industrial Law and about 4 from Taxation. Prepare both blocks.

Labour block: first learn the architecture (4 Codes replacing 29 Acts), then the IR Code (highest yield), then Wages, Social Security and OSH. Keep the old Act names in mind because many questions are still framed on them.

Tax block: learn constitutional basics (Arts 265, 246, 246A, 279A), then the five or six Income-tax ideas that recur (residence, heads of income, exemptions, TDS, assessment, appeals), then GST (supply, registration, ITC, returns, appeals).
Study the 'key_numbers' table in rapid revision: AIBE loves thresholds and time-limits.
AIBE is open-book: use the old-to-new concordance to find the right Code quickly.

Overlaps: Part 1 (Arts 14, 19(1)(c), 21, 23, 24, 43, 246A, 265, 279A, 300A), Part 2 (prosecution procedure), Part 7 (NI Act, Contract), Part 6 (Arbitration/ADR - stamp duty), Part 8 (Tort/Consumer; IP), Part 9 (PIL, Admin Law - delegated legislation, natural justice).

Thresholds moved: standing orders and prior-permission to 300 workers (from 100); factory definition 20 with power / 40 without power (from 10/20); contract-labour applicability 50 (from 20).
IR Code strike notice rule now covers all industrial establishments, not only public utility services.
Gratuity: 5 years continuous service, but not required in case of death or disablement; fixed-term employees qualify after 1 year.
Wage ceilings: bonus eligibility Rs 21,000; ESI wage limit Rs 21,000; EPF wage ceiling Rs 15,000.
A tax is a compulsory exaction without quid pro quo; a fee requires a service (Shirur Mutt).
Under GST, alcohol for human consumption is outside GST; petroleum products are outside until notified.
Income-tax 'Previous year / Assessment year' is replaced by a single 'Tax Year' only from Tax Year 2026-27.
Appeal limits: CIT(A) 30 days, ITAT 60 days, High Court (s.260A) 120 days; GST first appeal 3 months (+1).

sections.title: Architecture of Labour Law: Constitutional Basis, History and the Four Labour Codes
sections.articles: Arts 14, 16, 19(1)(c), 21, 23, 24, 39, 41, 42, 43, 43A; Entries 22-24 List III; the four Labour Codes
sections.overview: Why labour law looks the way it does, what the four Codes replaced, when they came into force and what remains outside them.
must_know: Constitutional basis: Fundamental Rights - Art 14 (equality; equal pay for equal work), Art 16 (public employment), Art 19(1)(c) (form unions, associations, cooperative societies; no fundamental right to strike), Art 21 (livelihood, dignity, health of workers), Art 23 (forced labour, begar), Art 24 (no child below 14 in hazardous work). DPSP - Art 38, 39(a),(d),(e),(f), 41 (right to work), 42 (just and humane conditions, maternity relief), 43 (living wage), 43A (workers' participation in management - 42nd Amendment), 43B (cooperatives). Seventh Schedule: Entry 22 (trade unions; industrial and labour disputes), Entry 23 (social security and social insurance; employment and unemployment), Entry 24 (welfare of labour incl. conditions of work, provident funds, employers' liability, workmen's compensation, invalidity and old-age pensions and maternity benefits) - all in the Concurrent List. Entry 55 List I (regulation of labour and safety in mines and oilfields); Entry 61 List I (industrial disputes concerning Union employees).

'Appropriate Government' under the Codes: Central Government for establishments such as railways, mines, oilfields, major ports, banking and insurance companies, central public-sector undertakings, air transport; State Governments for the rest.

Historical landmarks: Trade Disputes Act 1929; Trade Unions Act 1926; Industrial Disputes Act 1947 (framework for conciliation, adjudication and strikes); Industrial Employment (Standing Orders) Act 1946; Second National Commission on Labour (2002) recommended consolidation into broad groups - leading to the four Codes.

The four Labour Codes: (1) Code on Wages, 2019; (2) Industrial Relations Code, 2020; (3) Code on Social Security, 2020; (4) Occupational Safety, Health and Working Conditions Code, 2020. Passed in 2019-2020; Presidential assent 2019 (Wages) and 28 September 2020 (the other three). Brought into force by four notifications dated 21 November 2025, repealing 29 Central labour laws. Central Rules under all four Codes were notified on 8-9 May 2026; State rules are being notified in phases (several States have notified; some pending) [VERIFY State-wise status].

Counting the repeals (29 Acts): Wages Code subsumes 4 (Payment of Wages 1936; Minimum Wages 1948; Payment of Bonus 1965; Equal Remuneration 1976). IR Code subsumes 3 (Trade Unions 1926; Industrial Employment (Standing Orders) 1946; Industrial Disputes 1947). Social Security Code subsumes 9 (EPF & MP 1952; ESI 1948; Employees' Compensation 1923; Maternity Benefit 1961; Payment of Gratuity 1972; Employment Exchanges (CNV) 1959; Cine Workers Welfare Fund 1981; BOCW Welfare Cess 1996; Unorganised Workers' Social Security 2008). OSH Code subsumes 13 (Factories 1948; Mines 1952; Dock Workers (SHW) 1986; BOCW (RECS) 1996; Plantations Labour 1951; Contract Labour (R&A) 1970; Inter-State Migrant Workmen 1979; Working Journalists Acts 1955 and 1958; Motor Transport Workers 1961; Sales Promotion Employees 1976; Beedi & Cigar Workers 1966; Cine-Workers and Cinema Theatre Workers 1981).

Common features of the Codes: universal coverage (organised and unorganised sectors, with different thresholds); single registration and licence, online returns; Inspector-cum-Facilitator (a role of advice and inspection); web-based randomised inspections; fixed-term employment; written appointment letters; gender-neutral provisions; compounding of offences; decriminalisation of first offences in places; time-bound payment of wages; mandatory registration of gig and platform workers; national floor wage.

Laws that remain outside the Codes (examples): Child and Adolescent Labour (Prohibition and Regulation) Act 1986; Bonded Labour System (Abolition) Act 1976; Apprentices Act 1961; Employees' Pension Scheme 1995 (under the EPF scheme); Sexual Harassment of Women at Workplace (POSH) Act 2013; Rights of Persons with Disabilities Act 2016 (employment provisions); State Shops and Establishments Acts; Labour Welfare Fund Acts of States; Employees' Compensation is within the Social Security Code.

How AIBE may frame questions: (a) on the Codes (definitions, thresholds, repeals); (b) on old-Act case law that is still treated as good law (Bangalore Water Supply, Uma Devi); (c) on constitutional rights of workers. Because the Codes became operative only a year before the exam, expect questions that test 'which Act has been repealed' and 'what is the new threshold'.

Industrial jurisprudence principles: social justice and welfare orientation (Crown Aluminium Works v. Workmen, 1958); workers' right to collective bargaining; employer's right to manage; industrial peace through conciliation; 'hire and fire' limited by reasonableness and natural justice; reinstatement as ordinary relief for illegal termination.

key_provisions.content: 21 November 2025 (four notifications); Central Rules 8-9 May 2026.
Concurrent Legislative power over labour, social security and welfare.

sections.title: Industrial Relations Code, 2020 (I): 'Industry', 'Worker', 'Industrial Dispute', Employer, Bi-partite Forums and Trade Unions
sections.articles: IR Code ss.2-26 (replacing ID Act 1947 ss.2, Trade Unions Act 1926)
sections.overview: The definitions around which the whole of industrial law revolves. The nine-judge decision of 20 Aug 2026 on 'industry' is a high-probability current-affairs question.
must_know: The IR Code, 2020 consolidates and amends the law on trade unions, conditions of employment in industrial establishments or undertakings, and investigation and settlement of industrial disputes. It replaces the Trade Unions Act 1926, the Industrial Employment (Standing Orders) Act 1946 and the Industrial Disputes Act 1947.

'Industry' (IR Code s.2(p); ID Act s.2(j)): any systematic activity carried on by cooperation between an employer and worker (whether or not capital invested or profit motive) for production, supply or distribution of goods or services with a view to satisfy human wants or wishes (not spiritual or religious); includes any activity of the Dock Labour Board and activities relating to promotion of sales or business. Excluded: institutions owned or managed by organisations wholly or substantially engaged in charitable, social or philanthropic service; any activity of the appropriate Government relatable to sovereign functions (including defence research, atomic energy and space); domestic service; and any other activity notified. Compare s.2(j) ID Act - which was wide and the courts decided its limits.

Bangalore Water Supply and Sewerage Board v. A. Rajappa (1978, seven judges): 'triple test' - (i) systematic activity; (ii) organised by cooperation between employer and employee; (iii) for the production and/or distribution of goods and services calculated to satisfy human wants and wishes. Dominant nature test for composite institutions; hospitals, educational institutions, clubs, research institutes, charities with commercial activity may be industries; only strictly sovereign functions (those which only a sovereign can perform: legislation, administration of justice, maintenance of law and order, defence) and some charitable/ spiritual activities are excluded. It overruled the narrower view in Safdarjung Hospital v. Kuldip Singh Sethi (1970) and University of Delhi v. Ram Nath (1963). Earlier: Hospital Mazdoor Sabha (1960) (hospitals are industries); Corporation of City of Nagpur v. Employees (1960).

State of U.P. v. Jai Bir Singh (20 Aug 2026; 2026 INSC 897; nine judges led by CJI Surya Kant): the Court held by 6:3 that the reference was valid and, by 5:4, that the 1978 triple test needed refinement without overruling Bangalore Water Supply as a whole; the original 1978 test continues to govern all pending disputes under the repealed Industrial Disputes Act; the refined test will operate prospectively; and the Court said the 1978 expansive interpretation will not automatically govern s.2(p) of the IR Code, which has its own definition. Justice Nagarathna (reference not maintainable; definition should remain broad) and Justice Bagchi (reference valid; affirmed Bangalore Water Supply) wrote separate opinions; the outcome has been described as 4-4-1 on the merits [VERIFY the exact holdings from the judgment].

'Worker' (IR Code s.2(zr); ID Act 'workman' s.2(s)): any person (including apprentice - see exclusions; working journalists and sales promotion employees are included) employed in any industry to do any manual, unskilled, skilled, technical, operational, clerical or supervisory work for hire or reward, whether the terms are express or implied; includes a person dismissed, discharged or retrenched in connection with or as a consequence of an industrial dispute or whose dismissal, discharge or retrenchment has led to it; excludes members of the Armed Forces, police service or prison staff, persons mainly in managerial or administrative capacity, and persons in supervisory capacity drawing wages exceeding Rs 18,000 per month (or as notified) or exercising mainly managerial functions. The 'dominant nature of duties' test decides category (Burmah Shell Oil Storage v. Burmah Shell Management Staff Association, 1970; S.K. Maini v. Carona Sahu Co., 1994; Arkal Govind Raj Rao v. Ciba Geigy, 1985).

Employer-employee relationship: control and supervision test; integration test; economic reality; 'real employer' behind contractor (Hussainbhai v. Alath Factory Thozhilali Union, 1978; Balwant Rai Saluja v. Air India, 2014 - in contract labour, a contractor's workers become employees of principal employer only if the contract is a sham). 'Employer' under the Code includes the contractor, the legal representative of a deceased employer and, in a factory, the occupier. 'Industrial establishment' means an establishment where an industry is carried on.

'Industrial dispute' (IR Code s.2(q); ID Act s.2(k)): any dispute or difference between employers and employers, employers and workers or workers and workers connected with employment, non-employment, terms of employment or conditions of labour of any person; includes a dispute about discharge, dismissal, retrenchment or termination of an individual worker (individual dispute deemed an industrial dispute). A dispute must be espoused by a union or a substantial number of workers to be an 'industrial dispute' in the case of non-individual disputes (Workmen of Dimakuchi Tea Estate v. Dimakuchi Tea Estate, 1958). Dispute between an employee and an employer who is not within the definition of industry is not covered.

Bi-partite forums: Works Committee (IR Code s.3) in industrial establishments with 100 or more workers - equal number of employer and worker representatives, to promote measures for good relations; Grievance Redressal Committee (s.4) in every industrial establishment with 20 or more workers - up to ten members, equal representation of employer and workers, women proportionally; grievance must be raised within one year of cause; decision within 30 days; an aggrieved worker may seek conciliation within 30 days of the committee's decision [VERIFY section numbers].

Trade unions (Chapter III; replaces Trade Unions Act 1926): any combination of workers or employers for regulating relations or imposing restrictive conditions on conduct of trade or business, including federation. Registration: at least 7 members, and (in the case of an establishment) not less than 10% of workers or 100 workers, whichever is less - subject to a minimum of 7; Registrar of Trade Unions (State/Central); certificate of registration; union is a body corporate; immunity from criminal conspiracy (for agreement to do an act in furtherance of trade dispute) and civil suit for acts done in furtherance of a trade dispute; objects and funds (general and political fund - political activity only through a separate political fund and contributing members' consent); not more than one-third of office-bearers or five (whichever is less) may be outsiders; cancellation of registration by Registrar subject to appeal to Industrial Tribunal; unions may amalgamate.

Recognition of negotiating union (s.14): the union having 51% or more of the workers on the muster roll is the sole negotiating union; if no union has 51%, a negotiating council is constituted from unions with at least 20% membership, seats proportionate; the negotiating union/council negotiates with the employer on matters like wages and conditions and may be consulted on standing orders. A 'sole negotiating union' recognised by the employer from verification of membership by the employer or the appropriate Government.

Right to unionise: Art 19(1)(c) protects the right to form unions but not the right to recognition or to strike (All India Bank Employees' Association v. National Industrial Tribunal, 1962; Kameshwar Prasad v. State of Bihar, 1962; B.R. Singh v. Union of India, 1989). Union leaders enjoy limited protection; Rangarajan (2003) - no right to strike even for government employees.

Other basic terms: 'wages' for the Code (Section 2) - same as Code on Wages; 'appropriate Government'; 'average pay'; 'conciliation proceeding'; 'lay-off'; 'lock-out'; 'retrenchment'; 'strike'; 'trade union'; 'unfair labour practice' (appearing in the Code with a list in the Schedule [VERIFY]); 'fixed term employment' (see L4); 'standing orders'.

sections.title: Industrial Relations Code, 2020 (II): Standing Orders, Dispute Resolution Machinery, Strikes and Lock-outs
sections.articles: IR Code Chapters IV-VIII (ID Act ss.10-24; Standing Orders Act 1946)
sections.overview: How disputes are raised and resolved (conciliation, tribunals, arbitration), the 2020 changes (direct access to Tribunal, two-member Tribunal) and the strike/lock-out notice rules which now cover every industrial establishment.
must_know: Standing Orders (IR Code Chapter IV; replaces Industrial Employment (Standing Orders) Act 1946): apply to every industrial establishment with 300 or more workers (earlier 100); the employer must submit draft standing orders; model standing orders are prescribed by the Central Government (Model Standing Orders for manufacturing sector, and Model Standing Orders notified in 2026 [VERIFY]); certification by the Certifying Officer; deemed certification if no objection is raised within a prescribed time (about 60 days) [VERIFY]; appeal to the appellate authority; modifications only by agreement or by certification; matters provided in standing orders include classification of workers, manner of intimating working hours, holidays, pay-days, shift working, attendance, leave, conditions of discharge, termination, disciplinary action for misconduct, grievance redressal. Standing orders have statutory force (Western India Match Co. v. Workmen, 1973; U.P. State Road Transport Corp. v. Mohan Lal Gupta, 2000). Where standing orders do not exist, model standing orders apply.

Notice of change (Chapter V; ID Act s.9A): an employer who proposes to effect any change in conditions of service specified in the Schedule must give a 21-day notice to the workers affected; exceptions where change is under a settlement or award.

Dispute resolution machinery: Conciliation Officers appointed by the appropriate Government; the Industrial Tribunal (replacing Labour Courts and Tribunals of the ID Act) with two Members - one Judicial Member and one Administrative Member - and the National Industrial Tribunal for questions of national importance or interest to establishments in more than one State; Voluntary arbitration (Chapter VI; ID Act s.10A) by agreement of the parties to refer the dispute to arbitrator(s) before it is referred to Tribunal.

Raising a dispute (IR Code 2020): notice to the other party and to the conciliation officer; conciliation to be completed within a prescribed period (60 days); settlement in the course of conciliation is binding on the parties; if conciliation fails, the conciliation officer submits a failure report and parties may approach the Tribunal; under the Code, the party may approach the Tribunal directly after conciliation failure (no discretion of Government to make a 'reference' as under ID Act s.10) [VERIFY]. Individual disputes (discharge, dismissal, retrenchment, termination): a worker may apply to the conciliation officer and, if not settled within 45 days, to the Tribunal within two years from the date of discharge, dismissal, retrenchment or termination [VERIFY]. Tribunal awards: binding on the parties; enforcement as a decree; Tribunal's power to grant interim relief; powers of a civil court.

Section 11A ID Act (Tribunal's power to give appropriate relief in case of discharge or dismissal): where the Tribunal finds the punishment disproportionate, it may substitute a lesser punishment; Workmen of Firestone Tyre v. Management (1973); Delhi Transport Corporation v. D.T.C. Mazdoor Congress (1991) - 'hire and fire' rule; the employer must prove misconduct by fair domestic enquiry; if enquiry defective, employer may lead evidence before the Tribunal (Shankar Chakravarti v. Britannia Biscuit, 1979). Reinstatement with back wages is the general rule for illegal termination (Deepali Gundu Surwase v. Kranti Junior Adhyapak Mahavidyalaya, 2013); compensation in lieu is permitted in appropriate cases; the 'long delay/no back wages' approach in Allahabad Jal Sansthan v. Daya Shankar Rai (2005).

Strike and lock-out (IR Code Chapter VIII; ID Act ss.22-24): 'strike' - cessation of work by a body of persons employed in any industry acting in combination, or a concerted refusal or refusal under a common understanding to continue to work or accept employment; the Code expressly includes 'concerted casual leave on a given day by fifty per cent or more of the workers' as a strike. 'Lock-out' - temporary closing of a place of employment or suspension of work or refusal by an employer to continue to employ persons. Under the Code no person employed in an industrial establishment (not only a public utility service as under the ID Act) shall go on strike in breach of contract: (a) without giving notice of strike to the employer within sixty days before striking; (b) within fourteen days of giving such notice; (c) before the expiry of the date of strike specified in the notice; (d) during the pendency of conciliation proceedings before a conciliation officer and seven days after the conclusion; (e) during the pendency of proceedings before a Tribunal or National Tribunal and sixty days after the conclusion; (f) during the pendency of arbitration proceedings and sixty days after the conclusion; (g) during any period in which a settlement or award is in operation in respect of any of the matters covered. The same restrictions apply to lock-outs by employers (s.62) [VERIFY section number].

Legal and illegal strikes: illegal if in contravention of s.62; strike justified where employer's conduct is provocative; wages for strike period are denied unless strike is legal and justified (Crompton Greaves v. Workmen, 1978; Bank of India v. T.S. Kelawala, 1990). Lock-out must be bona fide. Participation in an illegal strike and incitement to strike are penalised. T.K. Rangarajan: government employees and others have no fundamental/statutory right to strike. Right to strike is a statutory right at best (Syndicate Bank v. K. Ramanujam, 1973; Ex-Capt. Harish Uppal v. Union of India, 2002 - lawyers strikes illegal).

Public utility services: ID Act s.2(n) list (e.g., railways, postal, telecom, power, water, sanitation, hospitals) and the Code's extension of notice to all; Essential Services Maintenance Acts (ESMA) of Central and State governments; Essential Services provisions; wage during strike. Compensation for lock-out/ strike in public utility.

Settlements and awards: settlement arrived at in conciliation binds all parties and workers; bipartite settlement (outside conciliation) binds signatories only; arbitration award; Tribunal award - enforceable by the Government; persons bound by award; commencement and period of operation (usually one year) ID Act s.19.

Powers of the appropriate Government: refer disputes (pre-Code); prohibit continuance of strike; give directions; prescribe thresholds by notification; exemption from provisions in public interest; appoint conciliation officers; set up Tribunals; Tribunals under the Code have the power of civil courts, can compound offences, and may grant relief to the worker for wrongful termination.

key_provisions.content: Notice of strike/lock-out: 60 days; not within 14 days of notice; and bars during conciliation/tribunal/arbitration - now for ALL industrial establishments.
Applies to industrial establishments with 300 or more workers.
Voluntary reference of disputes to arbitration.
Tribunal can modify punishment imposed by management.

sections.title: Industrial Relations Code, 2020 (III): Lay-off, Retrenchment, Closure, Fixed-term Employment, Re-skilling Fund, Unfair Labour Practices and Penalties
sections.articles: IR Code Chapters IX-XII (ID Act ss.2(kkk), 2(oo), 25A-25S, 25T-25U)
sections.overview: The most numerically testable block: notice, compensation, thresholds, deemed permission and the new Worker Re-skilling Fund.
must_know: Lay-off (ID Act s.2(kkk); IR Code Chapter IX): the failure, refusal or inability of an employer on account of shortage of coal, power or raw materials, accumulation of stocks, breakdown of machinery, natural calamity or any other connected reason to give employment to a worker whose name is on the muster roll and who has not been retrenched. Lay-off compensation: 50% of the total of basic wages and dearness allowance for all days of lay-off (other than weekly holidays) (ID Act s.25C; IR Code Chapter IX); not payable if the worker refuses alternative employment, does not present himself daily, or the lay-off is due to a strike or slowing down in another part of the establishment; not for more than 45 days in a year (then the employer may retrench) [VERIFY]. Lay-off provisions apply to establishments with 50 or more workers (but not seasonal).

Retrenchment (ID Act s.2(oo); IR Code): termination by the employer of the service of a worker for any reason whatsoever, otherwise than as a punishment inflicted by way of disciplinary action, except (a) voluntary retirement; (b) retirement on reaching the age of superannuation; (c) non-renewal of a contract of employment on its expiry (or termination under a stipulation in the contract); (d) termination due to continued ill-health (and, under the Code, non-renewal of fixed-term contract on expiry). The Constitution Bench in Punjab Land Development and Reclamation Corporation v. Presiding Officer, Labour Court (1990) read 'retrenchment' broadly to cover all terminations other than the stated exceptions (overruling the narrow view in Hariprasad Shivshankar Shukla v. A.D. Divelkar, 1957); State Bank of India v. N. Sundara Money (1976); Delhi Cloth & General Mills v. Shambhu Nath Mukherjee (1977).

Conditions precedent to retrenchment (IR Code s.70; ID Act s.25F): (a) one month's written notice indicating the reasons, or wages in lieu of notice; (b) compensation equivalent to fifteen days' average pay for every completed year of continuous service or any part thereof in excess of six months; (c) notice to the appropriate Government. Applies to workers who have completed one year of continuous service (240 days in the preceding 12 months - ID Act s.25B; Code uses 'one year of continuous service'). Non-compliance renders the retrenchment void ab initio and the worker is entitled to reinstatement (Santosh Gupta v. State Bank of Patiala, 1980; Mohan Lal v. Management of Bharat Electronics Ltd., 1981; Anoop Sharma v. Executive Engineer, 2010). Procedure for retrenchment (ID Act s.25G - last come first go): follow the rule of seniority within the category unless recorded reasons; re-employment of retrenched workers (s.25H): employer must give workers retrenched in the preceding year an opportunity to offer themselves for re-employment, with preference.

Worker Re-skilling Fund (IR Code s.83 [VERIFY]): employer shall credit 15 days' wages last drawn by the retrenched worker to the Worker Re-skilling Fund, from which the amount is paid to the worker's account within 45 days of retrenchment; in addition to retrenchment compensation.

Transfer of undertaking (ID Act s.25FF; Code): a worker is entitled to notice and compensation as if retrenched, unless the service is not interrupted, the terms are not less favourable and the new employer is legally liable for compensation.

Closure (ID Act s.2(cc); ss.25FFA, 25FFF): permanent closing down of a place of employment or part. Under ss.25FFA, an employer intending to close an undertaking employing 50 or more workers must give 60 days' notice to the appropriate Government; workers are entitled to notice and compensation as if retrenched (15 days' average pay for each year), but where the closure is due to unavoidable circumstances beyond the employer's control, compensation is capped at three months' average pay. Under Chapter X (special provisions - applicable to industrial establishments of 300 or more workers; earlier 100): prior permission of the appropriate Government is required for lay-off, retrenchment and closure (ID Act ss.25K-25S); application at least 90 days before closure; deemed permission if no response in 60 days; Government may grant permission, refuse or refer; effect of refusal; the Government can reduce or increase the 300-worker threshold by notification (IR Code s.77 [VERIFY]). The Code also provides that provisions of Chapter X apply to factory, mine or plantation - not to all industries.

Case law on prior permission: Excel Wear v. Union of India (1978) (s.25-O struck down as violating Art 19(1)(g)) - later Chapter VB (ss.25K-25S) upheld in Workmen of Meenakshi Mills v. Meenakshi Mills Ltd. (1992) (upheld ss.25N as reasonable restriction); Meenakshi Mills confirms that Chapter V-B is valid.

Fixed-term employment (IR Code s.2(o); ID Act and Standing Orders (Central) Rules amended 2018): a worker engaged on the basis of a written contract for a fixed period; the fixed-term worker has the same working hours, wages, allowances and other benefits as a permanent worker; entitled to gratuity pro rata even if service is less than five years (one year of service under SS Code); no notice or retrenchment compensation is payable on non-renewal at the end of the term; the employer may not use fixed-term contract to avoid regularisation of core work [VERIFY]. The Code adds flexibility; the judiciary examines abuse (e.g., Umadevi - see L8).

Unfair labour practices (ID Act ss.25T-25U and Fifth Schedule; IR Code retains a list of unfair labour practices by employers and trade unions [VERIFY]): to interfere with, restrain or coerce workers in exercising rights; to dominate or support a union (company union); discriminatory discharge; failure to implement awards; victimisation; employing badlis as casuals for years; to threaten strikes without notice; to coerce workers to join or not join a union; to incite or force go-slow; sit-down strikes; to indulge in acts of force or violence. Penalty: imprisonment up to 6 months or fine up to Rs 1,000 under the ID Act s.25U; under the Code, higher fines.

Offences and penalties: fines linked to contravention (strike/lock-out notice breaches, closure without notice, non-compliance with settlements); the Code decriminalises some offences with fines (Rs 10,000 to Rs 2 lakh in some cases, with imprisonment up to one month for aggravated cases [VERIFY]); compounding by the authority; offences by companies - officer in charge; courts of Metropolitan/ Judicial Magistrate; sections on cognizance only on complaint by or with the authority.

Termination of probationers, temporary workers and casuals: temporary or ad hoc employees can be retrenched but only following s.25F; sham fixed-term/casual appointments are scrutinised for unfair practice; regularisation is not automatic (Uma Devi, 2006).

key_provisions.content: Retrenchment: one month notice (or wages), compensation 15 days' average pay per year, notice to Government.
Prior permission for lay-off/retrenchment/closure in establishments with 300+ workers; deemed permission in 60 days.
Lay-off compensation - 50% of basic wages and DA.
Worker Re-skilling Fund - 15 days' wages.

Prior permission 300 workers; closure notice 60 days (50+ workers).
exam_traps: Compensation for lay-off is 50% of basic + DA; for retrenchment 15 days' average pay per year.
The one-month notice for retrenchment can be replaced by wages in lieu.
Closure compensation is limited to 3 months' average pay when due to unavoidable circumstances.
Prior permission requirement now begins at 300 workers (earlier 100).

How much lay-off compensation? (50% of basic wages and DA)
A fixed-term employee is eligible for gratuity after? (One year under the SS Code)
Notice period for closure of an undertaking employing 50+ workers? (60 days)

sections.title: Code on Wages, 2019: Wages, Minimum and Floor Wage, Payment, Bonus, Equal Remuneration
sections.articles: Code on Wages 2019 (subsumes Payment of Wages Act 1936; Minimum Wages Act 1948; Payment of Bonus Act 1965; Equal Remuneration Act 1976)
sections.overview: One law now covers payment of wages, minimum wages, bonus and equal pay for all employees. The 50% rule in 'wages', the floor wage and time-limits for payment are classic testing points.
must_know: Coverage: applies to all employees in all establishments (organised and unorganised); the earlier wage ceiling for the Payment of Wages Act (Rs 24,000 per month) has been removed - all employees are covered for timely payment of wages, deductions and minimum wages; bonus provisions apply to employees drawing wages up to Rs 21,000 per month.

'Wages' (s.2(y)): all remuneration whether by way of salary, allowances or otherwise, expressed in terms of money or capable of being so expressed, including basic pay, dearness allowance and retaining allowance. Excluded: bonus payable under any law; value of house accommodation, supply of light, water, medical attendance; employer's contribution to pension or provident fund and social security contribution; conveyance allowance; special expenses entitlement; house rent allowance; remuneration payable under award or settlement; overtime allowance; commission; gratuity; retrenchment compensation or other terminal benefits; travelling concession. If the excluded components together exceed 50% of total remuneration, the excess is added back to wages ('the 50% rule') - so basic pay and DA must form at least 50% of total remuneration. This definition governs PF, gratuity and bonus calculations under the Codes.

Equal remuneration (Chapter II, s.3): no employer shall discriminate on the ground of gender in matters of wages or recruitment, conditions of service and employment; includes transgender persons; employer shall not reduce the wages of any employee to comply. Randhir Singh v. Union of India (1982); State of Punjab v. Jagjit Singh (2016) - equal pay for equal work for temporary employees performing the same duties; Mackinnon Mackenzie & Co. v. Audrey D'Costa (1987) - Equal Remuneration Act principle; Air India v. Nargesh Meerza (1981).

Minimum wage: employers shall pay not less than the minimum wage prescribed - the Code applies minimum wages to all employees (not only scheduled employment). The Central Government fixes a 'floor wage' (s.9) having regard to living standards; the appropriate Government cannot fix a minimum wage below the floor wage; different minimum rates for different regions/skills; time-work, piece-work; review at intervals not exceeding five years; Advisory Boards; minimum wage includes basic wage and DA. Payment to non-employees via contractors - principal employer ultimately liable. Cases: Bijay Cotton Mills v. State of Ajmer (1955) - statutory minimum wage is a reasonable restriction under Art 19(1)(g); Unichoyi v. State of Kerala (1962) - inability to pay is no defence; Workmen v. Reptakos Brett & Co. (1992) - components of minimum wage; Sanjit Roy v. State of Rajasthan (1983) - minimum wages must be paid even in famine-relief works; PUDR (Asiad) (1982).
Hours of work and overtime: the appropriate Government fixes normal working day; overtime shall be paid at not less than twice the normal rate of wages (s.14); weekly rest day.

Payment of wages (Chapter III): wage period - daily, weekly, fortnightly or monthly (not exceeding one month); time-limit for payment (s.17): daily wage - at the end of the shift; weekly - on the last working day of the week; fortnightly - before the end of the second day after the end of the fortnight; monthly - before the expiry of the seventh day of the succeeding month; on removal, dismissal, retrenchment, resignation or superannuation - within two working days (s.17(2)); payment in coin/currency notes, cheque or credit to bank account or electronically ; responsibility for payment on the employer or a person designated; contractor/principal employer liability.

Deductions (s.18): only authorised deductions - fines, absence from duty, damage to goods, house accommodation, amenities, recovery of advances, income-tax, court orders, cooperative society subscriptions, insurance premiums etc.; total deductions shall not exceed 50% of wages in any wage period (s.18(2)); fines limited and with show-cause; no deduction for damage unless caused by neglect/default.

Bonus (Chapter V): every employee drawing wages not exceeding Rs 21,000 per month and who has worked for at least 30 days in an accounting year is entitled to bonus; minimum bonus is 8.33% of wages earned or Rs 100, whichever is higher; maximum 20% of wages; calculation ceiling of Rs 7,000 or the minimum wage, whichever is higher; allocable surplus (60% of available surplus for companies; 67% for others); set-on and set-off; payment within eight months from close of accounting year; disqualification for fraud, riotous or violent behaviour, theft, misappropriation or sabotage; establishments newly set up exempt for the first five accounting years unless profits; Mumbai Kamgar Sabha v. Abdulbhai Faizullabhai (1976) - bonus is not deferred wage but a share in profits; the Full Bench Formula governs the determination of allocable surplus in bonus disputes.

Claims and adjudication: employee may apply to the Authority (appointed by the appropriate Government) for unpaid wages/bonus within three years from the date on which the claim arose [VERIFY section number]; penalty up to ten times the amount in some cases; interest; appeals to Appellate Authority within 30 days; recovery as arrears of land revenue. 'Inspector-cum-Facilitator' appointed to supply information and advice and to inspect; web-based random inspection.

Penalties and compounding: offence of paying less than the minimum wage - fine up to Rs 50,000 for first offence; repeat within five years - imprisonment up to three months and/or fine up to Rs 1 lakh [VERIFY]; Code offences compoundable by the authority with the specified amounts; no imprisonment for first-time minor offence.

key_provisions.content: Definition of 'wages' - 50% rule.
Prohibition of discrimination on the ground of gender.
Floor wage set by the Central Government.
Overtime at not less than twice the normal rate.
Time-limit for payment: monthly - before 7th day; on termination - within 2 working days.
Deductions; total not to exceed 50% of wages.
Bonus: 8.33% minimum - 20% maximum; wage ceiling Rs 21,000.

landmark_cases.held: Minimum wage law is a reasonable restriction in public interest.

landmark_cases.case: Unichoyi v. State of Kerala
landmark_cases.held: Employer must pay the statutory minimum even if the industry is unable to pay.

landmark_cases.case: PUDR v. Union of India (Asiad Workers)
landmark_cases.held: Wages below minimum amount to forced labour.

landmark_cases.case: Randhir Singh v. Union of India
landmark_cases.held: Equal pay for equal work - Art 14, 16, 39(d).

landmark_cases.case: State of Punjab v. Jagjit Singh
landmark_cases.held: Temporary employees doing the same work as regular employees entitled to equal pay.

landmark_cases.case: Mumbai Kamgar Sabha v. Abdulbhai Faizullabhai
landmark_cases.held: Bonus is linked to profits and is not an enforceable claim to deferred wage in the absence of statute.

landmark_cases.case: Sanjit Roy v. State of Rajasthan
landmark_cases.held: Famine relief work - minimum wages must be paid; exemption unconstitutional.

mnemonics: Wages: 50% rule - excluded items beyond 50% are added back.
Bonus: 8.33% - 20%; ceiling Rs 21,000; 30 working days.
exam_traps: House rent allowance, bonus, gratuity, overtime and employer's PF contribution are excluded from 'wages' - but the 50% rule may add some back.
Total deductions are capped at 50% of wages.
On termination or resignation, wages must be paid within two working days.
Minimum wage applies to all employees under the Code, not only scheduled employment.
probable_questions: Under the Code on Wages, overtime is payable at what rate? (Twice the normal rate)
What is the minimum bonus percentage? (8.33%)
Which Act dealt with 'equal remuneration' earlier? (Equal Remuneration Act 1976)
Maximum deductions from wages? (50%)

sections.title: Code on Social Security, 2020: EPF, ESI, Gratuity, Maternity Benefit, Employees' Compensation, Gig and Platform Workers
sections.overview: Thresholds, eligibility and benefits under the nine-Act merger. Gig and platform worker provisions are new and topical.
must_know: The Code subsumes: Employees' Compensation Act 1923; ESI Act 1948; EPF and Miscellaneous Provisions Act 1952; Employment Exchanges (Compulsory Notification of Vacancies) Act 1959; Maternity Benefit Act 1961; Payment of Gratuity Act 1972; Cine Workers Welfare Fund Act 1981; Building and Other Construction Workers' Welfare Cess Act 1996; Unorganised Workers' Social Security Act 2008. Administered by the EPFO, ESIC, National Social Security Board for unorganised, gig and platform workers, and the Social Security Fund.

Employees' Provident Fund (Chapter III): applies to establishments with 20 or more employees (Central Government may lower the threshold or extend to others); mandatory contributions by employer and employee at 12% of wages (rate can be lower for certain establishments); statutory wage ceiling for compulsory coverage Rs 15,000 per month; three schemes - EPF Scheme 1952, Employees' Pension Scheme 1995 (EPS) and Employees' Deposit Linked Insurance Scheme 1976 (EDLI); Universal Account Number; interest on deposits declared annually; EPFO; damages for delayed payment; recovery as arrears of land revenue. 'Basic wage' for PF - Bridge and Roof Co. v. Union of India (1963); Manipal Academy of Higher Education v. Provident Fund Commissioner (2008); Vivekananda Vidya Mandir v. Regional Provident Fund Commissioner (2019) - special allowances that are universally paid are part of basic wage; Surya Roshni Ltd. v. EPF (2019).

Employees' State Insurance (Chapter IV): applies to establishments with 10 or more employees (and the Code allows extension to hazardous employment even with fewer, and to establishments with less than 10 on a voluntary basis); employees drawing wages up to Rs 21,000 per month (Rs 25,000 for persons with disabilities); contributions - employer 3.25% and employee 0.75% of wages; benefits - sickness, maternity, disablement (temporary and permanent), dependants' benefit, medical benefit, funeral expenses, unemployment allowance (Atal Bimit Vyakti Kalyan Yojana); ESI Corporation. Under the Code, disputes concerning employer liability are heard by the Social Security Appellate Tribunal instead of ESI Courts [VERIFY].

Gratuity (Chapter V; formerly Payment of Gratuity Act 1972): payable on termination of employment after continuous service of five years or more - on superannuation, retirement or resignation, or death or disablement due to accident or disease (no minimum period needed in case of death or disablement). Applies to establishments with 10 or more employees (and to factories, mines, oilfields, plantations, ports, railways, shops and establishments). Fixed-term employees qualify on a pro-rata basis after one year of continuous service (Code). Formula: 15 days' wages (last drawn) for each completed year of service = (last drawn monthly wages x 15 / 26) x number of years (seasonal establishments: 7 days per season); employer's liability ceiling Rs 20 lakh (as notified). Gratuity must be paid within 30 days of becoming payable; simple interest on delay; nomination; exemption from attachment. Forfeiture: wholly or partly if services are terminated for wilful omission or negligence causing damage or loss to employer's property (to the extent of loss), or for riotous or disorderly conduct or an act of violence, or for an offence involving moral turpitude committed in the course of employment. Cases: Union Bank of India v. C.G. Ajay Babu (2018) - gratuity cannot be forfeited merely on departmental misconduct; offence involving moral turpitude must be established; Jeewanlal (1929) Ltd. v. Appellate Authority (1984) - gratuity payable irrespective of whether employer is making profits; the Controlling Authority decides disputes; appeal to Appellate Authority within 60 days.

Maternity benefit (Chapter VI; formerly Maternity Benefit Act 1961 as amended in 2017): applies to every establishment employing 10 or more persons; woman must have worked at least 80 days in the 12 months preceding the expected delivery; benefit is paid at the average daily wage for the period of actual absence; duration: 26 weeks (not more than 8 weeks before the expected delivery) for the first two children; 12 weeks (6 weeks pre-delivery) for a third or subsequent child; 12 weeks for an adopting mother (child below three months) and a commissioning mother (from date child handed over); miscarriage or medical termination: 6 weeks; tubectomy: 2 weeks; illness arising out of pregnancy: 1 month; nursing breaks (two breaks of 15 minutes); work from home option after the benefit period if the nature of work permits; crèche mandatory for establishments with 50 or more employees (visits allowed four times a day); medical bonus of Rs 3,500 if no pre/post-natal care provided by employer [VERIFY amount]; protection from dismissal during maternity. Cases: Municipal Corporation of Delhi v. Female Workers (Muster Roll) (2000) - daily wagers are entitled; Neera Mathur v. LIC (1992) - questions on pregnancy history in application invalid; Deepika Singh v. Central Administrative Tribunal (2022) - maternity leave (and child care leave) for women with step-children; Dr Kavita Yadav v. Secretary, Ministry of Health (Delhi HC, 2023) - maternity benefits to contractual employees.

Employees' Compensation (Chapter VII; formerly Employees' Compensation Act 1923, earlier Workmen's Compensation Act): employer is liable to pay compensation when an employee suffers personal injury by accident arising out of and in the course of employment or contracts an occupational disease listed in Schedule III; compensation for death (50% of monthly wages x relevant factor, subject to a minimum), permanent total disablement (60% x relevant factor, minimum), partial disablement and temporary disablement; liability not arising if the disablement does not exceed three days (except death/serious), employee under influence of drugs/alcohol, wilful disobedience of safety order, wilful removal of a safety device; interest at 12% (or as notified) if compensation not paid within one month; penalty up to 50% for default without sufficient cause; claim to be made within two years of accident; Commissioner for Employees' Compensation adjudicates; appeal to High Court only on substantial question of law. Notional extension of employment: Saurashtra Salt Manufacturing Co. v. Bai Valu Raja (1958); Mackinnon Mackenzie & Co. v. Ibrahim Mahomed Issak (1969); Employees' State Insurance Corp. v. Francis De Costa (1996); Pratap Narain Singh Deo v. Srinivas Sabata (1976) - 'accident' includes injury arising from an event that is unexpected.

Gig workers and platform workers (Chapter IX): 'gig worker' - person who performs work or participates in a work arrangement outside the traditional employer-employee relationship; 'platform worker' - a gig worker whose work is based on online platform; 'aggregator' - digital intermediary or marketplace for buyers and sellers (e.g., ride-hailing, food delivery). Aggregators must contribute 1% to 2% of their annual turnover (capped at 5% of the amount paid or payable to gig and platform workers) to the Social Security Fund; benefits via schemes - life and disability insurance, health and maternity benefits, old-age protection; registration on the e-Shram portal with Aadhaar-linked UAN; eligibility based on a minimum number of days of engagement (e.g., 90 days with one aggregator or 120 days across aggregators in the draft rules) [VERIFY Central Rules 2026]. State laws: Rajasthan Platform Based Gig Workers (Registration and Welfare) Act 2023; Karnataka Platform-based Gig Workers (Social Security and Welfare) Act 2025 [VERIFY]. The Code does not decide whether gig workers are 'employees' for other labour laws.

Unorganised workers and welfare: National Social Security Board; Welfare schemes (Pradhan Mantri Shram Yogi Maandhan; Ayushman Bharat; e-Shram); BOCW Welfare Boards - cess on cost of construction (1%-2%) funds the welfare of building and construction workers; Cine Workers Welfare Fund; Employment Exchanges (National Career Service portal) and mandatory notification of vacancies (now through National Career Service for establishments with 20+ employees [VERIFY]).

Common features: the Code makes provision for social security for fixed-term workers, inter-state migrant workers (portability), and extends EPF/ESI to more sectors; 'wages' as in the Code on Wages; 'employee' defined broadly (includes contract and unorganised workers); Facilitator inspections; penalties for non-compliance (fines and imprisonment for diverting contributions); the Code allows aggrieved persons to appeal to the Appellate Tribunal.

key_provisions.content: 5 years' service (1 year for fixed-term employees); 15 days' wages per year; cap Rs 20 lakh.
26 weeks for first two children; 12 weeks for third or adopting/commissioning mother.
Aggregator contribution 1%-2% of turnover capped at 5% of payouts.
20 employees; ESI threshold 10; wage ceilings Rs 15,000 (EPF) / Rs 21,000 (ESI).

Maternity: 26 weeks (1st & 2nd child); 12 weeks (3rd+, adoption, commissioning).
exam_traps: Gratuity requires 5 years' continuous service, but this is not needed in case of death or disablement.
Maternity 26 weeks applies only to the first two children.
EPF threshold is 20 employees; ESI 10 employees.
The 'Employees' Compensation Act' is now merged into the Code - but claims on pre-Code accidents may still use old provisions.

Gratuity is payable after how many years of continuous service? (5)
Which Code now regulates gig and platform workers? (Code on Social Security 2020)
ESI contribution rates? (Employer 3.25%, employee 0.75%)

sections.title: Occupational Safety, Health and Working Conditions Code, 2020; Contract Labour; Inter-State Migrants; Child and Bonded Labour; Women at Work
sections.articles: OSH Code 2020 (13 Acts); Child and Adolescent Labour Act 1986; Bonded Labour System (Abolition) Act 1976; POSH Act 2013; Arts 23, 24
sections.overview: Safety, health, working hours, contract labour and the constitutional rights cases (child labour, bonded labour, Vishaka, Bhopal, absolute liability).
must_know: OSH Code subsumes 13 Acts: Factories Act 1948; Mines Act 1952; Dock Workers (Safety, Health and Welfare) Act 1986; Building and Other Construction Workers (RECS) Act 1996; Plantations Labour Act 1951; Contract Labour (Regulation and Abolition) Act 1970; Inter-State Migrant Workmen (RECS) Act 1979; Working Journalists and other Newspaper Employees (Conditions of Service) and Miscellaneous Provisions Act 1955; Working Journalists (Fixation of Rates of Wages) Act 1958; Motor Transport Workers Act 1961; Sales Promotion Employees (Conditions of Service) Act 1976; Beedi and Cigar Workers (Conditions of Employment) Act 1966; Cine-Workers and Cinema Theatre Workers (Regulation of Employment) Act 1981.

Applicability: establishments with 10 or more workers (mines and docks irrespective of numbers); 'factory' means premises where 20 or more workers are employed (with power) or 40 or more (without power) (earlier 10 and 20 respectively; State Governments may raise the limit further); a single registration of an establishment; 'occupier' - the person with ultimate control over the affairs of the establishment (in a company, one of the directors); 'Inspector-cum-Facilitator'; 'Chief Inspector'; National and State Occupational Safety and Health Advisory Boards.

Employer duties: provide a workplace free from hazards; appointment letters for all workers; free annual health check-up for workers above a certain age (45 years) [VERIFY]; Safety Committee in factories with 500 or more workers [VERIFY]; Welfare Officer in factories with 500 or more workers; canteen for 100 or more workers; crèche for 50 or more workers; first-aid; occupational disease notification; compensation for accidents is under the Social Security Code; notify accidents. Hazardous processes: duties for hazardous factories (Bhopal lessons - Chapter on hazardous industries; Environment Protection Act 1986; Public Liability Insurance Act 1991; National Green Tribunal Act 2010).

Working hours and leave: 8 hours a day and 48 hours a week (more flexible hours if prescribed); spread-over of 12 hours; overtime wages at not less than twice the rate (Wages Code), overtime ceiling per quarter [125 hours - VERIFY]; weekly day of rest; annual leave with wages: one day for every 20 days worked (earlier 240 days eligibility is relaxed to 180 days of work in the preceding calendar year); women may work night shifts (7 pm - 6 am) with consent and prescribed safety measures (transport, security, CCTV, restrooms); women in mines and hazardous work allowed with safeguards.

Contract labour (Chapter XI): the Code applies to establishments and contractors employing 50 or more contract workers (earlier 20); the contractor must hold a licence (a single, all-India licence valid for five years, with relaxations); contract labour is prohibited in core activities of an establishment except where (i) the normal functioning is such that the work is ordinarily done through contractors; (ii) the activities do not require full-time workers for the major part of the working hours in a day; or (iii) there is a sudden increase in volume of work; the principal employer is liable to pay wages and benefits if the contractor defaults; workers must be paid wages and have facilities (canteen, rest rooms, drinking water). Steel Authority of India Ltd. v. National Union Water Front Workers (2001, Constitution Bench): on abolition of contract labour, absorption of contract workers in the principal employer is not automatic; Air India Statutory Corporation v. United Labour Union (1996) overruled in part; Balwant Rai Saluja v. Air India (2014): 'control' test - contract labour is the principal employer's employee only if the contract is a sham; Gujarat Electricity Board v. Hind Mazdoor Sabha (1995).

Inter-State migrant workers: includes a worker who migrates on his own and not only through a contractor; employer must pay an annual 'journey allowance' for to-and-fro travel to the native place; portability of benefits (ration, PDS); registration on the national portal; ISMW displacement allowance (as under old Act) is dropped in favour of journey allowance.

Women at work: Maternity (Social Security Code); equal pay (Wages Code s.3); Sexual Harassment of Women at Workplace (Prevention, Prohibition and Redressal) Act 2013 - Internal Committee (10+ employees), Local Committee (district); complaint within 3 months (extendable); inquiry 90 days; Vishaka v. State of Rajasthan (1997); Medha Kotwal Lele v. Union of India (2013) - compliance; Apparel Export Promotion Council v. A.K. Chopra (1999); Aureliano Fernandes v. State of Goa (2023) - proper constitution of Internal Committee; Air India v. Nargesh Meerza (1981) - unequal service conditions for air hostesses (retirement on pregnancy) held arbitrary; Anuj Garg v. Hotel Association of India (2008) - ban on women employees in bars struck as stereotyping; Charu Khurana v. Union of India (2015) - no gender bias in make-up artists' union membership.

Child labour: Art 24 (no child below 14 in factory/mine/hazardous employment); Child and Adolescent Labour (Prohibition and Regulation) Act 1986 as amended in 2016 - complete prohibition of employment of children below 14 in all occupations (with an exception for family enterprises and audio-visual entertainment outside school hours); prohibition of adolescents (14-18) in hazardous occupations/processes; penalties; Right to Education Act 2009 (Art 21A) - cross-ref Part 1. Cases: M.C. Mehta v. State of Tamil Nadu (1996) - Sivakasi: directions on child labour (Rs 20,000 compensation per child; child labour rehabilitation-cum-welfare fund); Bachpan Bachao Andolan v. Union of India (2011) - circus children, trafficking; People's Union for Democratic Rights v. Union of India (1982).

Bonded labour: Art 23; Bonded Labour System (Abolition) Act 1976 abolishes the system and extinguishes debts; District Magistrate as implementing authority; vigilance committees; rehabilitation; offences punishable with up to 3 years' imprisonment and fine up to Rs 2,000; Bandhua Mukti Morcha v. Union of India (1984); Neerja Chaudhary v. State of M.P. (1984) - rehabilitation is part of liberation; Central Sector Scheme for Rehabilitation of Bonded Labourers (2021).

Penalties and compounding in the OSH Code: higher fines for fatal accidents, with compensation to victims; first offence of certain kinds can be compounded; offences by companies attract liability of the officers in charge; a court of Metropolitan Magistrate or Judicial Magistrate of the First Class tries offences; cognizance only on a complaint by or with the authority of Inspector-cum-Facilitator.

Absolute liability and workplace disasters: M.C. Mehta v. Union of India (Oleum Gas Leak, 1987) - absolute liability for hazardous industry (departure from Rylands v. Fletcher); Union Carbide Corp. v. Union of India (1989) - Bhopal settlement; Union of India v. Union Carbide (1991) - review; Consumer Education and Research Centre v. Union of India (1995) - right to health of workers is a part of Art 21 (asbestos); Occupational diseases and ESI; Charan Lal Sahu v. Union of India (1990) - Bhopal Gas Leak (Processing of Claims) Act 1985 upheld.

Applies to establishments with 50 or more contract workers; core-activity prohibition with exceptions.
8 hours a day; 48 hours a week; overtime double; women night work with consent.
No child below 14 in hazardous employment.

sections.title: Judicial Principles in Labour Law: Regularisation, Termination, Contract Workers, Domestic Enquiry, Strikes and Constitutional Rights of Workers
sections.articles: Arts 14, 16, 19, 21, 311; ID Act s.11A; Code principles
sections.overview: Principles you will need to apply to a fact scenario.
must_know: Regularisation: Secretary, State of Karnataka v. Umadevi (3) (2006, Constitution Bench): courts cannot order regularisation of employees appointed irregularly or without following the constitutional scheme of public employment (Arts 14, 16); 'illegal' v. 'irregular' appointments; one-time measure for those who had served 10 years or more against sanctioned posts. Later: Jaggo v. Union of India (Dec 2024) and Shripal v. Nagar Nigam, Ghaziabad (Jan 2025): the Supreme Court criticised the misuse of Umadevi to deny regularisation to long-serving workers on perennial work and directed regularisation; the principle that 'temporary' labels cannot disguise permanent needs [VERIFY].

Equal pay for equal work: Randhir Singh (1982); State of Punjab v. Jagjit Singh (2016) - temporary employees doing the same work as regular employees get minimum of regular pay scale; contrary caution in State of Haryana v. Charanjit Singh (2006).

Disciplinary proceedings and domestic enquiry: principles of natural justice - notice, opportunity, impartial inquiry officer; no bias; findings supported by evidence; 'some evidence' and not strict rules of evidence (State of Haryana v. Rattan Singh, 1977); punishment proportional (Ranjit Thakur v. Union of India, 1987; Union of India v. G. Ganayutham, 1997 - proportionality as part of Wednesbury); Tribunal's power under s.11A ID Act; supply of enquiry report before punishment (Managing Director, ECIL v. B. Karunakar, 1993); suspension and subsistence allowance (State of Maharashtra v. Chandrabhan, 1983); termination simpliciter of probationers (Dipti Prakash Banerjee v. Satyendra Nath Bose National Centre, 1999 - stigma test).

Standing Orders and misconduct: acts of misconduct defined in standing orders; 'misconduct' wider than enumerated list (Glaxo Laboratories v. Presiding Officer, 1984 - standing orders must be certified; employer cannot punish for acts not covered).

Hire and fire: Delhi Transport Corporation v. DTC Mazdoor Congress (1991) - arbitrary termination clauses unconstitutional for State instrumentalities; Central Inland Water Transport Corp. v. Brojo Nath Ganguly (1986) - unconscionable contract of service void under s.23 Contract Act and Art 14.

Reinstatement with back wages: Deepali Gundu Surwase (2013); J.K. Synthetics v. K.P. Agrawal (2007) (reinstatement not automatic); Gauri Shankar v. State of Rajasthan (2015) - compensation in lieu; Allahabad Jal Sansthan (2005).

Strike: T.K. Rangarajan (2003) - no fundamental right; all strikes subject to statutory rules; illegal strike; wages not payable unless justified; Harish Uppal (2002); dismissals for participation in illegal strike - limited to violence.

Constitutional rights of workers: Art 19(1)(c) - protects formation of unions, not recognition; Art 21 - livelihood (Olga Tellis; Delhi Transport Corp.); Art 23 - forced labour (PUDR); Art 14 - equal pay; Art 16 - public employment; Art 43A workers' participation in management; Art 300A and wages - PF/gratuity as property.

Employer-employee relationship tests - control and supervision, integration, economic reality, multiple factors; 'contract of service' v. 'contract for services' (Dharangadhara Chemical Works v. State of Saurashtra, 1957; Silver Jubilee Tailoring House v. Chief Inspector of Shops, 1974); platform workers - emerging law: Karnataka and Rajasthan Acts; international: Uber (UK Supreme Court 2021) as a comparative marker.
Compounding and prosecution: offences under labour law are triable by Magistrates; limitation for cognizance is as prescribed under the Code; a complaint by Inspector; 'sanction'.

key_provisions.content: Equality in public employment - basis of Umadevi.
Tribunal's power to substitute punishment.
Participation of workers in management.

Back wages are not automatic in every case.

sections.title: Constitutional Framework of Taxation and General Principles of Tax Law
sections.overview: Who can tax what; limits on taxing power; tax v. fee; interpretation of taxing statutes; tax avoidance v. evasion.
must_know: Art 265: no tax shall be levied or collected except by authority of law - the foundation; requires a valid statute (not executive order) and a valid collection (2026 Supreme Court cases reaffirm that tax cannot be retained or collected without authority of law). Art 246 with the Seventh Schedule distributes taxing powers; Art 246A (101st Amendment, 2016) - special provision for GST: Parliament and State Legislatures have simultaneous power; Parliament has exclusive power over inter-State supply (Art 269A). Art 279A: GST Council.

Union List (List I) tax entries: Entry 82 - taxes on income other than agricultural income; Entry 83 - duties of customs including export duties; Entry 84 - duties of excise on tobacco and other goods manufactured or produced (post-GST confined to petroleum crude, high-speed diesel, motor spirit, natural gas, aviation turbine fuel and tobacco products); Entry 85 - corporation tax; Entry 86 - taxes on the capital value of assets (excluding agricultural land); Entry 88 - taxes other than stamp duties on... (estate duty omitted/not levied); Entry 89 - terminal taxes on goods or passengers carried by railway, sea or air; Entry 91 - rates of stamp duty in respect of bills of exchange, cheques, promissory notes, bills of lading, letters of credit, policies of insurance, transfer of shares, debentures, proxies and receipts; Entry 97 - residuary (taxes not in lists).

State List (List II) tax entries: Entry 45 - land revenue; Entry 46 - taxes on agricultural income; Entry 47 - duties in respect of succession to agricultural land; Entry 48 - estate duty on agricultural land; Entry 49 - taxes on lands and buildings; Entry 50 - taxes on mineral rights subject to limitations imposed by Parliament by law relating to mineral development; Entry 51 - duties of excise on alcoholic liquors for human consumption and opium, Indian hemp and other narcotic drugs (but not medicinal and toilet preparations); Entry 52 - taxes on the entry of goods into a local area for consumption, use or sale (octroi - subsumed by GST); Entry 54 - taxes on the sale or purchase of goods other than newspapers (now limited to petroleum products and alcohol for human consumption after GST); Entry 55 - taxes on advertisements other than in newspapers; Entry 56 - taxes on goods and passengers carried by road or inland waterways; Entry 57 - taxes on vehicles; Entry 58 - taxes on animals and boats; Entry 59 - tolls; Entry 60 - taxes on professions, trades, callings and employments; Entry 61 - capitation taxes; Entry 62 - taxes on entertainment, amusements, betting and gambling (local); Entry 63 - rates of stamp duty on documents other than those in List I.

Art 276: tax on professions, trades, callings and employments - maximum Rs 2,500 per person per year (by the 60th Amendment 1988). Art 268 - stamp duties and excise on medicinal and toilet preparations levied by Union but collected and appropriated by States; Art 269 - taxes on consignment/ sale of goods in inter-State trade (Union levied, assigned to States); Art 269A - GST on inter-State supply levied and collected by the Government of India and apportioned between Union and States by the GST Council recommendations; Art 270 - taxes levied by the Union and distributed between the Union and States (income tax other than agricultural, and GST (CGST)); Art 271 - Parliament may levy a surcharge for Union purposes only; Art 275 and 282 grants; Art 280 Finance Commission (16th FC - Chairman Arvind Panagariya - award period 2026-31); Art 285 - exemption of Union property from State taxation; Art 289 - State property exempt from Union taxation (except trade or business of the State); Art 286 - restrictions on State taxes on sale or purchase of goods outside the State and in the course of import/export; Art 287-288 (electricity; water).

101st Amendment (2016) and GST: introduced Art 246A, 269A, 279A, Entry 54 amended; the 'goods and services tax' defined in Art 366(12A) (tax on supply of goods or services or both except alcoholic liquor for human consumption); GST on petroleum crude, HSD, motor spirit, natural gas and ATF applies from the date notified by Council on recommendation (not yet). GST Council: Union Finance Minister (Chairperson), Union Minister of State in charge of Revenue, State Ministers in charge of Finance; quorum one-half of members; decisions by three-fourths of weighted votes (Centre one-third, States two-thirds); recommendations are persuasive, not binding (Union of India v. Mohit Minerals Pvt. Ltd., 2022). [Cross-ref Part 1.]

Tax, fee and cess: tax - compulsory exaction for public purposes without any specific quid pro quo; fee - payment for specific services rendered with a broad correlation (Commissioner, Hindu Religious Endowments v. Sri Lakshmindra Thirtha Swamiar of Sri Shirur Mutt, 1954); fee must be related to the cost of service in a broad sense (Kewal Krishan Puri v. State of Punjab, 1979); a cess is a tax levied for a specific purpose; surcharges are additional taxes. Retrospective taxation is permissible but subject to Arts 14, 19, 20(1); Vodafone International Holdings B.V. v. Union of India (2012) - indirect transfer of shares of a foreign company not taxable in India under the law then in force; the Finance Act 2012 retrospective amendment (Explanation to s.9(1)(i)) was later withdrawn by the Taxation Laws (Amendment) Act 2021 (no demands for pre-2012 indirect transfers).

Interpretation: charging provisions are strictly construed - 'there is no equity about a tax' (Cape Brandy Syndicate v. IRC, 1921); ambiguity in charging provision is resolved in favour of the assessee, but in exemption notifications, ambiguity is resolved in favour of the Revenue (Commissioner of Customs v. Dilip Kumar & Co., 2018, Constitution Bench); machinery provisions are construed liberally; contemporanea expositio; 'look at' not 'look through' (Vodafone); substance over form in avoidance cases: CIT v. McDowell & Co. (1985) (colourable devices not allowed) but Union of India v. Azadi Bachao Andolan (2003) (tax planning is legitimate within the framework of law); GAAR (Chapter X-A, ss.95-102) effective 1 April 2017; Judicial anti-avoidance rule.

Tax evasion (illegal), tax avoidance (legal but defeating the purpose) and tax planning (within law). Tax and Article 14: classification for taxation allowed with wide latitude (R.K. Garg v. Union of India, 1981; East India Tobacco v. State of A.P., 1962); Art 19(1)(g): tax cannot be confiscatory; Art 20(1): no retrospective penalty; Art 300A: property and tax.

Delegated taxation: essential legislative function (levy) cannot be delegated; rate-fixing may be delegated within guidelines (Hamdard Dawakhana v. Union of India, 1960; Gwalior Rayon Mfg. v. Assistant Commissioner of Sales Tax, 1974); delegated legislation is effective only on publication per statute (Viraj Impex v. Union of India, 2026 [VERIFY]); tax statutes and 'law' - Art 265.

Tax tribunals: ITAT (constituted under s.252 of the Income-tax Act 1961); CESTAT; GST Appellate Tribunal (GSTAT, s.109 CGST Act); Authority for Advance Ruling; Settlement Commission replaced by Interim Board for Settlement (2021); Dispute Resolution Committee; Tribunals Reforms Act 2021 and the L. Chandra Kumar principle - tribunals subject to High Court's writ jurisdiction (cross-ref Part 1).

key_provisions.content: No tax except by authority of law.
Concurrent power on GST (inter-State supply: Parliament only).
Professional tax cap: Rs 2,500 per annum.
Taxes on income other than agricultural income (Union).
Taxes on agricultural income (State).
States' property exempt from Union taxation except for trade.

landmark_cases.held: 'Look at' the transaction; indirect transfer outside India not taxable; retrospective amendment followed and later repealed.

landmark_cases.case: R.K. Garg v. Union of India
landmark_cases.held: Economic and fiscal legislation gets wide latitude under Art 14.

landmark_cases.held: GST Council recommendations are not binding.

landmark_cases.held: Nine judges (8:1): States can tax mineral rights; royalty is not a tax.

mnemonics: Union: income (82), customs (83), corporation tax (85). State: agri income (46), land/buildings (49), profession (60).
Professional tax cap: Rs 2,500.
exam_traps: Agricultural income tax is a State subject (Entry 46, List II); income tax on all other income is Union (Entry 82, List I).
Alcohol for human consumption is outside GST; the State levies excise on it (Entry 51 List II) and VAT (Entry 54).
GST Council recommendations are not binding on Parliament or State Legislatures.
Surcharge can be levied only by the Union for its own purposes (Art 271).
