sections.title: Income-tax: Basic Concepts, Residential Status, Heads of Income, Exemptions, Deductions and Rates
sections.articles: Income-tax Act 1961 ss.2-80; Income-tax Act 2025 (from 1 April 2026)
sections.overview: Concepts a legal aspirant is expected to know: 'person', 'income', previous year, residence, five heads, important exemptions, deductions, capital gains rates and slabs.
must_know: Income-tax Act 2025: replaces the Income-tax Act 1961 from 1 April 2026; 'Tax Year' replaces the dual concept of 'previous year' and 'assessment year' (the first Tax Year is 2026-27); fewer sections and chapters than the 1961 Act (the 2025 Act has 536 sections, 23 chapters and 16 schedules [VERIFY]); new regime slabs now in s.202 [VERIFY]; the substance of tax law is largely retained. Income earned in Financial Year 2025-26 is assessed in AY 2026-27 under the 1961 Act; Tax Year 2026-27 (FY 2026-27) is the first under the 2025 Act. Proceedings for earlier years continue under the 1961 Act by savings. Examination papers in 2026-27 may use either; understand both.

Charge (s.4 of 1961 Act): income-tax is charged on the total income of the previous year of every person at the rates fixed by the annual Finance Act. 'Person' (s.2(31)): an individual, a Hindu undivided family, a company, a firm, an association of persons or body of individuals, a local authority, and every artificial juridical person. 'Assessee' (s.2(7)): person by whom any tax or other sum is payable. 'Income' (s.2(24)): an inclusive definition covering profits and gains, dividend, voluntary contributions, perquisites, capital gains, winnings from lotteries etc. 'Previous year' (s.3): the financial year immediately preceding the assessment year (1 April - 31 March); 'assessment year' (s.2(9)): the 12 months commencing 1 April following the previous year. Agricultural income (s.2(1A)): rent or revenue from land used for agriculture; income from operations on agricultural produce; farm building - exempt from income-tax under s.10(1) (but taken into account for rate purposes under 'partial integration').

Residential status (s.6): an individual is resident if (a) he is in India for 182 days or more in the previous year; or (b) he is in India for 60 days or more in the previous year and 365 days or more in the four preceding years. Exceptions: for an Indian citizen or person of Indian origin leaving India for employment abroad or as crew, the 60-day limit is replaced by 182 days; for a citizen or PIO who visits India with total income (other than foreign sources) exceeding Rs 15 lakh, the limit is 120 days (and 365 days in the four preceding years). Deemed resident (s.6(1A)): an Indian citizen having total income (other than foreign source) exceeding Rs 15 lakh who is not liable to tax in any other country. Resident but not ordinarily resident (RNOR): non-resident in 9 of the 10 preceding years or has been in India for 729 days or less in the 7 preceding years. A Hindu undivided family or firm is resident unless control and management are wholly outside India. A company is resident if it is an Indian company or its place of effective management (POEM) in that year is in India (s.6(3)). Tax incidence: resident and ordinarily resident - global income; RNOR - income received/accruing in India and income from a business controlled in or profession set up in India; non-resident - income received or accruing/deemed to accrue in India.

Scope of total income (s.5) and deemed accrual (s.9): income deemed to accrue or arise in India includes income through a business connection in India, property, asset or source of income in India, transfer of a capital asset situated in India (including indirect transfers - Explanation 5), salary for services rendered in India, interest/royalty/fees for technical services payable by residents; 'significant economic presence' rules (Explanation 2A to s.9(1)(i)) for digital businesses.

Heads of income (s.14): (1) Salaries (ss.15-17) - standard deduction Rs 75,000 under new regime (Rs 50,000 under old); perquisites; leave encashment; gratuity exemption. (2) Income from house property (ss.22-27) - annual value; standard deduction 30% of net annual value; interest on housing loan (s.24(b)) up to Rs 2 lakh for self-occupied property (old regime). (3) Profits and gains of business or profession (ss.28-44) - allowable deductions (s.30-37), depreciation (s.32), presumptive taxation (ss.44AD, 44ADA, 44AE), disallowances (s.40, 40A), tax audit (s.44AB) for turnover over Rs 1 crore (Rs 10 crore if cash transactions under 5%). (4) Capital gains (ss.45-55A): gains on transfer of capital asset; short-term if held 24 months or less (12 months or less for listed securities and equity-oriented funds); long-term otherwise; exemptions in ss.54, 54B, 54EC, 54F; cost of acquisition; indexation withdrawn for transfers after 23 July 2024. (5) Income from other sources (ss.56-59): dividend, interest, gifts exceeding Rs 50,000 from non-relatives (s.56(2)(x)), winnings from lotteries and games, family pension.

Capital gains rates (FY 2025-26, applicable from 23 July 2024): short-term capital gains on listed equity shares and equity-oriented mutual funds where STT is paid - 20% (s.111A); long-term capital gains on listed equity - 12.5% on gains exceeding Rs 1.25 lakh (s.112A); long-term capital gains on other assets - 12.5% without indexation (s.112); STCG on other assets - at slab rates. Securities Transaction Tax (STT) levied under Chapter VII of the Finance (No.2) Act 2004.

Exempt incomes (s.10): agricultural income; allowances for HRA and LTA (subject to rules); gratuity (limits); amount received on maturity of life insurance (subject to s.10(10D) conditions); scholarships; share of profit from a firm; dividend from Indian companies is taxable (post-2020); income of a local authority; political party income (s.13A) subject to conditions; charitable and religious trusts (ss.11-13) - registration under s.12AB; Section 10(1) agricultural; PPF interest.

Deductions from gross total income (Chapter VI-A; available in the old regime and some in new): s.80C (up to Rs 1.5 lakh - life insurance, PPF, ELSS, tuition fees, repayment of home loan principal, NSC); 80CCD(1B) (additional Rs 50,000 NPS); 80D (health insurance premium up to Rs 25,000, Rs 50,000 for senior citizens); 80E (interest on education loan - no limit); 80G (donations); 80GG (rent); 80TTA/80TTB (savings account interest up to Rs 10,000; Rs 50,000 for seniors); 80U (disability); 80CCD(2) (employer NPS contribution - allowed in new regime too). Under the default new regime (s.115BAC), most Chapter VI-A deductions and exemptions are not allowed except 80CCD(2) and a few.

Set-off and carry forward (ss.70-80): intra-head and inter-head set-off; house property loss set-off limited to Rs 2 lakh per year against other heads; carry forward of business loss for 8 years, capital loss for 8 years, speculative loss for 4 years; unabsorbed depreciation indefinitely. Clubbing (ss.60-64): income of spouse (remuneration from concern in which the other spouse has substantial interest), minor child's income (s.64(1A)), transfer of asset to spouse without adequate consideration - clubbed with the transferor's income.

Individual slabs - FY 2025-26 (AY 2026-27): New regime (default; s.115BAC): up to Rs 4 lakh - nil; Rs 4-8 lakh - 5%; Rs 8-12 lakh - 10%; Rs 12-16 lakh - 15%; Rs 16-20 lakh - 20%; Rs 20-24 lakh - 25%; above Rs 24 lakh - 30%. Rebate under s.87A (new regime): full rebate for total income up to Rs 12 lakh (maximum Rs 60,000), effectively no tax up to Rs 12.75 lakh of salary income with the standard deduction. Old regime (opt-in): up to Rs 2.5 lakh - nil (Rs 3 lakh for senior citizens, Rs 5 lakh for super seniors); Rs 2.5-5 lakh - 5%; Rs 5-10 lakh - 20%; above Rs 10 lakh - 30%; rebate up to Rs 12,500 for income up to Rs 5 lakh. Health and education cess: 4% on tax plus surcharge. Surcharge for incomes above Rs 50 lakh; capped at 25% in the new regime. Slabs for Tax Year 2026-27 under the 2025 Act continue as above unless changed by the Finance Act 2026 [VERIFY].

Corporate tax: domestic company - 22% (plus surcharge 10% and cess 4% = 25.17%) under s.115BAA if it forgoes exemptions/incentives; 25% for companies with turnover not exceeding Rs 400 crore (earlier regime); 30% otherwise; new manufacturing companies s.115BAB (15%) expired for those commencing production after 31 March 2024; foreign companies 35% plus surcharge; Minimum Alternate Tax (MAT) 15% of book profit under s.115JB (not applicable to s.115BAA companies); partnership firms and LLPs 30%; cooperative societies 22%/25%/30%. Alternate Minimum Tax (AMT) for non-corporate assessees (s.115JC) 18.5%.

Important concepts: 'agricultural income' is exempt; 'casual income' (lotteries, crossword puzzles) is taxed at 30% flat (s.115BB); 'unexplained cash credits' (s.68) taxed at 60% plus surcharge/cess (s.115BBE); 'gifts' (s.56(2)(x)) - exempt from relatives; 'dividend' taxable at slab rates; 'perquisites' as per Rules 3; 'salary' includes basic, DA, bonus, commission, advance; 'income from undisclosed sources'; 'income by deeming' - s.69 etc. Landmark: Navinchandra Mafatlal v. CIT (1954) - 'capital gains' covers transfer of shares; Sumati Dayal v. CIT (1995) - real income and human probabilities; K.P. Varghese v. ITO (1981) - burden under s.52 is on the Revenue; CIT v. Durga Prasad More (1971) - benami/ real nature of transactions.

key_provisions.content: Charge of income-tax on total income of the previous year.
Residential status: 182 days or 60 days + 365 days in preceding four years.
Five heads of income: Salaries; House property; PGBP; Capital gains; Other sources.
Default new tax regime; basic exemption Rs 4 lakh; s.87A rebate up to Rs 12 lakh income.
Deduction up to Rs 1.5 lakh (old regime).

mnemonics: Five heads: 'S-H-B-C-O' - Salaries, House property, Business/Profession, Capital gains, Other sources.
Residence: 182 days OR (60 + 365 days in last 4 years).
exam_traps: Agricultural income is exempt but included for rate purposes in some cases.
Tax Year replaces 'previous year/assessment year' only from FY 2026-27 under the 2025 Act.

sections.title: Income-tax Procedure: TDS, Advance Tax, Returns, Assessment, Search, Appeals, Penalties and Prosecution
sections.overview: Collection (TDS, advance tax), returns, scrutiny and reassessment, appellate hierarchy and criminal provisions.
must_know: PAN (s.139A) is compulsory for specified transactions; linking with Aadhaar (s.139AA) upheld in Binoy Viswam v. Union of India (2017) subject to the limitation that it cannot apply to persons without Aadhaar. TAN for tax deductors.

Tax deduction at source (TDS) (Chapter XVII-B): principle of 'pay as you earn'; s.192 - salary (at average rate); s.193 - interest on securities; s.194 - dividends (10%); s.194A - interest other than on securities (10%, threshold Rs 50,000 for banks and Rs 1 lakh for senior citizens from FY 2025-26 [VERIFY]); s.194C - payments to contractors (1% individual/HUF; 2% others); s.194I - rent (2% for machinery and 10% for land/building); s.194J - professional or technical fees (10%; 2% for technical services); s.194Q - purchase of goods exceeding Rs 50 lakh (0.1%); s.195 - payments to non-residents; s.206AA - higher TDS rate of 20% if PAN is not furnished; s.206C - TCS (tax collected at source) on specified goods and transactions. Deductor must deposit TDS by the 7th of the next month, issue TDS certificates (Form 16/16A), and file quarterly returns; failure leads to disallowance (s.40(a)(ia)), interest (s.201(1A)) and penalty; prosecution for failure to deposit TDS (s.276B). Under the 2025 Act, the TDS provisions are consolidated in s.393 [VERIFY].

Advance tax (ss.207-211): payable if estimated tax liability for the year is Rs 10,000 or more; due in instalments: 15% by 15 June; 45% by 15 September; 75% by 15 December; 100% by 15 March; presumptive taxpayers under s.44AD/44ADA pay in a single instalment by 15 March; interest under ss.234B (default in advance tax) and 234C (deferment of instalments) at 1% per month; s.234A interest for delay in filing return.

Returns: s.139(1) - due date for individuals not requiring audit: 31 July; companies and persons requiring audit: 31 October; transfer pricing cases: 30 November; belated return s.139(4) up to 31 December of the assessment year (with fees under s.234F); revised return s.139(5); updated return s.139(8A) - within 24 months from the end of the assessment year (extended to 48 months by the Finance Act 2025 [VERIFY]) on payment of additional tax of 25% or 50%; return not required for those below taxable limit except specified conditions. Under the 2025 Act the due dates are by reference to the 'tax year'.

Assessments: processing of return - s.143(1) (intimation; adjustments), done by Centralised Processing Centre; scrutiny assessment - notice under s.143(2) must be served within three months from the end of the financial year in which the return is filed; assessment order under s.143(3); best judgment assessment - s.144 (non-compliance); faceless assessment scheme - s.144B; reassessment - ss.147-151: s.148A mandatory inquiry and show-cause; notice under s.148 within three years from the end of the assessment year, extendable up to 10 years where the income escaping assessment is Rs 50 lakh or more represented in assets or expenditure (s.149); sanction by specified authority; Union of India v. Ashish Agarwal (2022) and Union of India v. Rajeev Bansal (2024) - treatment of reassessment notices issued after 1 April 2021 under the old regime and TOLA relaxation; the Finance Act 2026 reportedly restored a Joint Assessing Officer/ section 147A route with retrospective effect, and the Supreme Court in Sept 2026 stayed a Punjab and Haryana High Court decision striking it down [VERIFY]. Limitation for completing assessment: s.153 (9 months from the end of the assessment year in which the income was first assessable - for scrutiny assessments) [VERIFY].

Search, seizure and survey: s.132 - search and seizure authorised by Principal Director/ Director General/ Chief Commissioner on 'reason to believe' based on information; panchnama; seizure; presumption under s.132(4A) that books/documents found belong to the person; s.133A - survey (no seizure; limited power to impound); s.131 - powers of civil court (summons, examination on oath). Courts have held search must follow strict procedure; Pooran Mal v. Director of Inspection (1974) - illegal search does not invalidate seized material; ITO v. Seth Brothers (1969) - 'reason to believe'.

Appeals: first appeal to the Commissioner of Income-tax (Appeals) (now National Faceless Appeal Centre) under s.246A within 30 days of service of the demand/order (s.249); second appeal to the Income Tax Appellate Tribunal under s.253 within 60 days of receipt of the CIT(A)'s order (s.253(3)) - ITAT is the final fact-finding authority; appeal to the High Court under s.260A only on a substantial question of law within 120 days; appeal to the Supreme Court under s.261 (certificate of fitness) or by Special Leave Petition under Art 136. Dispute Resolution Panel (s.144C) for eligible assessees (foreign companies, transfer pricing cases). Revision: s.263 - Principal Commissioner can revise an order that is erroneous and prejudicial to the interest of the Revenue (within two years from end of financial year in which order was passed); s.264 - revision in favour of the assessee (within one year). Rectification of mistake apparent from the record - s.154 (within four years from the end of the financial year). Vivad se Vishwas Scheme 2024; Interim Board for Settlement; Board for Advance Rulings.

Penalties: s.270A - under-reporting of income: 50% of tax payable on under-reported income; misreporting: 200%; s.271AAB (search cases); s.271B (failure to get books audited); s.271F (failure to file return); s.272A and s.272B (default in complying with notices / PAN); s.271C (failure to deduct TDS); penalty orders appealable to CIT(A). Prosecution (Chapter XXII): s.276B - failure to pay TDS to Government: rigorous imprisonment of 3 months to 7 years plus fine; s.276C(1) - wilful attempt to evade tax: if the tax evaded exceeds Rs 25 lakh - 6 months to 7 years; otherwise 3 months to 2 years; s.276CC - wilful failure to furnish return: same thresholds; s.277 - false statement in verification; s.278 - abetment; s.278E - presumption of culpable mental state (accused must prove absence); s.279 - sanction by Principal Commissioner/Commissioner for prosecution; s.279(2) - compounding of offences. Offences are triable by Magistrates (Chapter XXII).

Black Money (Undisclosed Foreign Income and Assets) and Imposition of Tax Act 2015: undisclosed foreign income taxed at 30% plus penalty at 90% (total about 120%); prosecution for wilful failure to disclose foreign assets: imprisonment 6 months to 7 years; Benami Transactions (Prohibition) Act 1988 as amended in 2016: benami transactions prohibited; confiscation; Union of India v. Ganpati Dealcom Pvt. Ltd. (2022) - section 3(2) (criminal provisions) unconstitutional (manifestly arbitrary) and the 2016 amendment operating prospectively; 'tax evasion' under Prevention of Money Laundering Act as a scheduled offence.

Transition to the 2025 Act: tax year; sections renumbered; 'tax year' for all new proceedings after 1 April 2026; ITR forms and rules (Income-tax Rules 2026 [VERIFY]); the Act retains scheme of heads, residence, TDS, assessment; old pending cases decided under the 1961 Act. For AIBE, remember: 1961 Act section numbers for case law; use the 'tax year' language for the 2025 Act.

key_provisions.content: Due dates: 31 July (non-audit), 31 October (audit), 30 November (transfer pricing).
Advance tax: 15%, 45%, 75%, 100% (15 Jun / 15 Sep / 15 Dec / 15 Mar).
Scrutiny notice within 3 months from the end of the financial year of filing the return.
Appeals: CIT(A) 30 days; ITAT 60 days; High Court 120 days (substantial question of law).
Penalty: 50% (under-reporting) / 200% (misreporting).
Wilful tax evasion: 6 months-7 years if tax evaded exceeds Rs 25 lakh.

sections.title: GST (I): CGST/IGST Framework, Supply, Levy, Registration, Composition, Input Tax Credit, Returns and Rates
sections.overview: The legal architecture of GST, the concept of 'supply', registration thresholds, composition scheme, ITC conditions and blocked credits, returns, and GST 2.0 rates.
must_know: GST laws: Central GST Act 2017, Integrated GST Act 2017, Union Territory GST Act 2017, GST (Compensation to States) Act 2017 (compensation cess withdrawn after GST 2.0), and State GST Acts. Effective 1 July 2017. Dual GST: CGST + SGST on intra-State supply; IGST on inter-State supply and imports (IGST on import under Customs Tariff Act s.3(7)). Destination-based consumption tax; tax levied on 'supply'.

Levy (CGST s.9): GST on all intra-State supplies of goods or services or both (except alcoholic liquor for human consumption) at rates notified by the Government on recommendation of the Council, on the transaction value (s.15); not exceeding 20% (CGST) per the Act. Reverse charge: s.9(3) (notified goods/services) and s.9(4) (supplies by unregistered to registered persons, restricted to notified classes); e-commerce operator liable under s.9(5) for notified services.

Supply (CGST s.7): includes all forms of supply of goods or services such as sale, transfer, barter, exchange, licence, rental, lease or disposal made or agreed to be made for a consideration by a person in the course or furtherance of business; import of services for a consideration whether or not in the course of business; and activities specified in Schedule I made without consideration (permanent transfer or disposal of business assets with ITC; supply between related persons or distinct persons in the course of business; supply by principal to agent and vice versa; import of services from a related person outside India). Schedule II classifies activities as supply of goods or services (e.g., transfer of title in goods - goods; lease/ licence - services; works contract - services; renting of immovable property - services; temporary transfer of IPR - services). Schedule III - activities neither a supply of goods nor services (services by an employee to employer in the course of employment; court fees; functions of MPs, MLAs, panchayat members; funeral services; sale of land and (subject to para 5(b) of Schedule II) completed buildings; actionable claims other than lottery, betting and gambling). Composite supply (two or more supplies naturally bundled; tax by principal supply) and mixed supply (tax by the supply attracting the highest rate) - s.8.

Time, value and place of supply: time of supply of goods (s.12) - earlier of date of invoice or last date on which invoice should be issued, or date of payment; services (s.13); value of supply (s.15) - transaction value (price actually paid or payable where parties are not related and price is the sole consideration), plus taxes, incidental expenses, interest; place of supply determines whether supply is intra-State or inter-State (IGST Act ss.10-13); zero-rated supplies - exports and supplies to SEZ (IGST s.16) - refund of ITC or IGST paid.

Taxable person and registration (s.22): every supplier is liable to be registered if aggregate turnover in a financial year exceeds Rs 40 lakh (goods), Rs 20 lakh (services); for special category States Rs 20 lakh (goods) and Rs 10 lakh (services) [thresholds unchanged by GST 2.0 - VERIFY]. Compulsory registration regardless of turnover (s.24): inter-State suppliers of goods, casual taxable persons, persons liable under reverse charge, non-resident taxable persons, e-commerce operators and persons supplying through them, input service distributors, persons deducting TDS/collecting TCS, online information and database access suppliers. Registration within 30 days of becoming liable; PAN-based; GSTIN of 15 digits; cancellation (s.29).

Composition levy (s.10): option for registered persons with aggregate turnover up to Rs 1.5 crore (Rs 75 lakh for special category States) in preceding year to pay tax at a lower rate (1% for manufacturers and traders; 5% for restaurants; 6% for specified service providers up to Rs 50 lakh under s.10(2A)); cannot make inter-State supply, cannot collect tax from customers, cannot claim ITC, not available to e-commerce operators and supplier of notified goods (ice cream, pan masala, tobacco) [verify rates].

Input Tax Credit (ss.16-21): ITC is allowed for tax paid on inward supplies used or intended to be used in the course or furtherance of business; conditions (s.16(2)): (a) possession of a tax invoice or debit note or other prescribed documents; (b) receipt of goods or services; (c) tax actually paid to the Government by the supplier (either in cash or through ITC); (d) filing of returns under s.39; and (aa) the details are communicated in GSTR-2B (inserted 2022). Time limit (s.16(4)): invoice-based credit may be availed up to 30 November following the end of the financial year or the date of filing the annual return, whichever is earlier (extended for certain years under amnesty and Finance Act 2024 [VERIFY]). Blocked credits (s.17(5)): motor vehicles for transport of persons having seating capacity of not more than thirteen (with exceptions); vessels and aircraft (with exceptions); food and beverages, outdoor catering, beauty treatment, health services, cosmetic and plastic surgery, membership of club/health and fitness centre, rent-a-cab, life insurance and health insurance (except where obligatory/ taxable outward); travel benefits to employees on vacation; works contract services for construction of immovable property (other than plant and machinery) except where input is for further works contract/ construction; goods or services used for personal consumption; goods lost, stolen, destroyed, written off or disposed of by gift or free samples; tax paid under ss.74, 129, 130. Apportionment of credit for exempt supplies (s.17(1), (2) and Rules 42-43). Matching under s.41 (provisional credit - omitted; GSTR-2B invoice-matching now).

Safari Retreats Pvt. Ltd. v. Chief Commissioner of CGST (3 Oct 2024): 'plant or machinery' in s.17(5)(d) must be tested by the functionality test (whether the building is itself the plant used for making outward supply, e.g., hotels, malls); the Court held that a mall's building rented out can be a 'plant' on facts only if it is essential to the activity; the Finance Act 2025 retrospectively replaced 'plant or machinery' with 'plant and machinery' in s.17(5)(d) with effect from 1 July 2017 to neutralise the decision; a review petition was dismissed (2025) and later High Court/ Supreme Court decisions continue to apply the functionality test for 'plant' [VERIFY].

Returns (ss.37-48): GSTR-1 (outward supplies; due 11th of next month or quarterly for QRMP), GSTR-3B (summary return and payment; 20th of next month), GSTR-9 (annual return; 31 December of next year), GSTR-9C reconciliation statement for large taxpayers; GSTR-2A/2B auto-generated statements; TDS (s.51 - 2% by notified government departments on payments exceeding Rs 2.5 lakh); TCS (s.52 - e-commerce operators 0.5% of net value of taxable supplies); electronic ledgers (cash, credit, liability); e-invoicing mandatory for taxpayers with aggregate turnover above Rs 5 crore; e-way bill for consignments exceeding Rs 50,000 in value (Rule 138).

Rates (GST 2.0 - Council's 56th meeting 3 Sept 2025; effective 22 September 2025): the four-slab structure (5%, 12%, 18%, 28%) was replaced by two principal slabs - 5% (merit) and 18% (standard) - and a special 40% rate for sin and luxury goods (tobacco and pan masala, aerated drinks, high-end cars, etc.); special low rates for precious metals and stones (0.25%, 1.5%, 3%) continue; many items moved from 12%/28% to 5%/18%; essentials and certain health/education items exempt or at nil; individual life and health insurance premium exempted; compensation cess was phased out as loans were repaid and the tobacco/pan masala items moved to 40% [VERIFY].

Alcohol for human consumption outside GST (State excise and VAT); petroleum crude, HSD, motor spirit, natural gas, ATF outside GST until notified; electricity outside; transitional - 'GST on tobacco' plus central excise on tobacco products. Remedies for GST compliance: GST Practitioners; GSTN as common portal.

Key case law: Union of India v. Mohit Minerals (2022) - Council recommendations not binding; Union of India v. VKC Footsteps India (2021) - refund of accumulated ITC due to inverted duty structure available only on input goods, not input services (Rule 89(5)) - upheld; Safari Retreats (2024); Mohit; also decisions on retrospective amendments and Rule 86B (restriction on ITC use) [VERIFY 2026 rulings: Bhandari Scrap Traders (ITC where supplier did not pay tax), Tata Steel (limitation under s.74)].

key_provisions.content: Scope of 'supply' - Schedules I, II, III.
Levy and collection; reverse charge.
Eligibility and conditions for ITC; 30 November time limit.
Blocked credits.
Registration: Rs 40 lakh (goods) / Rs 20 lakh (services); special category Rs 20/10 lakh.
Composition scheme up to Rs 1.5 crore turnover.

landmark_cases.held: Functionality test for 'plant' in s.17(5)(d); ITC on construction of building used for renting not automatically blocked.

landmark_cases.held: Right to rectify GST returns / carry forward credit recognised in the context of technical glitches [VERIFY].

mnemonics: GST: 'CGST + SGST (intra-State); IGST (inter-State); UTGST (UT).'
Rates after 22 Sept 2025: 5% / 18% / 40% (plus special rates).
Registration threshold: Rs 40 lakh goods; Rs 20 lakh services.
exam_traps: Composition scheme cannot be used for inter-State supplies or by e-commerce operators.
Schedule III items (e.g., sale of land) are neither goods nor services - no GST.
Alcohol for human consumption is outside GST.
ITC time limit: 30 November following the end of the FY or date of annual return, whichever earlier.

Registration threshold for goods suppliers (normal States)? (Rs 40 lakh)
After 22 September 2025, which GST slabs exist? (5%, 18%, and 40% special)
ITC is blocked on motor vehicles with seating capacity of not more than? (13 persons)

sections.title: GST (II): Assessment, Demand and Recovery, Refunds, Appeals (GSTAT), Offences and Penalties
sections.overview: Procedures after registration and return filing: refunds, assessment, audit, demand under s.73/74/74A, the appeal hierarchy ending with GSTAT, and offences with monetary thresholds.
must_know: Refund (s.54): application within two years from the 'relevant date' (date of export, date of filing return, etc.); refund of tax paid on zero-rated supplies, inverted duty structure, excess payment, unutilised ITC; unjust enrichment bar (refund of incidence passed on to consumers is credited to Consumer Welfare Fund); interest on delayed refund.

Assessment (Chapter XII): self-assessment (s.59); provisional assessment (s.60); scrutiny of returns (s.61); assessment of non-filers (s.62) - best judgment; assessment of unregistered persons (s.63); summary assessment in special cases (s.64) - to protect Revenue. Audit (s.65 - by tax authorities; s.66 - special audit by chartered accountant/cost accountant). Inspection, search and seizure (s.67) - by authorised officer on reasons to believe (Commissioner's authorisation); inspection of goods in movement (s.68; e-way bill); power to arrest (s.69) - Commissioner may authorise arrest where reason to believe that a person has committed an offence specified in s.132(1)(a),(b),(c) or (d) which is punishable under s.132(1)(i) or (ii) (i.e., offences above Rs 5 crore or fake invoice) - such offences are cognizable and non-bailable; offence cognizable and non-bailable where tax evaded exceeds Rs 5 crore. Arrest must follow the Cr.P.C. (now BNSS) procedure (s.69(3)); anticipatory bail is available (Radhika Agarwal v. Union of India, 2025 - the Supreme Court upheld the validity of ss.69 and 132 but held that arrest powers must be exercised on 'reasons to believe' that are recorded and that safeguards of the Cr.P.C. apply).

Demand and recovery: s.73 (non-fraud cases - tax not paid, short paid, erroneous refund or wrongly availed/utilised ITC) - notice within two years and nine months from the due date for annual return; order within three years of that date; payment of tax and interest within 30 days avoids penalty; s.74 (fraud, wilful misstatement or suppression of facts) - notice within four years and six months; order within five years; penalty equal to tax; s.74A (inserted by the Finance Act 2024; effective from FY 2024-25) - unified provision for all cases with a uniform time-limit (notice within 42 months and order within 12 months of notice for the 'non-fraud' type; 54 months for fraud type [VERIFY]). s.75 general provisions (opportunity of hearing; adjournment up to three times; no demand beyond show-cause notice); s.76 tax collected but not deposited; s.77-78 (payment of tax; recovery within 3 months of order); s.79 (modes of recovery - attachment and sale, etc.); s.80 (instalments). Interest (s.50) 18% on delayed payment; 24% on undue/excess ITC claim; late fee (s.47).

Penalty (ss.122-129): s.122 - for specified offences (supply without invoice, fake invoice, ITC fraud): penalty of Rs 10,000 or tax evaded whichever is higher; s.125 - general penalty up to Rs 25,000; s.129 - detention, seizure and release of goods in transit (200% of tax for taxable goods; 2% of value or Rs 25,000 for exempt goods); s.130 - confiscation of goods or conveyance; s.126 - no penalty for minor breaches (Rs 5,000 limit); s.127 - general penalty provisions.

Offences and prosecution (s.132): tax evasion of more than Rs 5 crore - imprisonment up to five years plus fine; Rs 2 crore to Rs 5 crore - up to three years; Rs 1 crore to Rs 2 crore - up to one year; fake invoice or ITC fraud (issue of invoices without supply) - up to five years if tax involved exceeds Rs 5 crore; the offence is non-bailable where tax amount exceeds Rs 5 crore; cognizable when exceeding Rs 5 crore; s.132(5) - cognizable and non-bailable; s.132(4); prior sanction by Commissioner; compounding under s.138 (not for offences relating to fake invoices); s.134 - cognizance only with Commissioner's sanction.

Appeals: first appeal to the Appellate Authority (Joint/Additional Commissioner (Appeals)) under s.107 within three months from the date of communication of the order (the Appellate Authority may condone delay up to one month); pre-deposit - full of the admitted tax plus 10% of the disputed tax (maximum Rs 25 crore for CGST and Rs 25 crore for SGST); second appeal to the GST Appellate Tribunal (GSTAT) under s.112 within three months (extendable by 3 months) - pre-deposit additional 10% of the disputed tax (max Rs 20 crore each for CGST and SGST) in addition to the amount paid under s.107; appeal to the High Court under s.117 on a substantial question of law within 180 days; appeal to the Supreme Court under s.118. Revisional authority (s.108) and the Advance Ruling Authority (ss.95-98; Appellate Authority for Advance Ruling).

GSTAT: constituted under s.109 CGST Act as amended by the Finance Act 2023; National Bench (Principal Bench) at New Delhi; State Benches at several cities; operationalised in 2025 - the Government notified the Tribunal in September 2025, appointments of President and Members were made, and the portal for filing appeals went live; the Council extended the period to file legacy appeals in respect of orders passed before the Tribunal began functioning; a relaxed limitation window extends to 31 December 2026 for such cases [VERIFY]. GSTAT hears appeals from orders of the Appellate Authority and Revisional Authority; cases involving only issue of place of supply go directly to the National Bench; the Tribunal is subject to the principle in L. Chandra Kumar.

Advance ruling (ss.95-106): binding on the applicant and the concerned officer; for a question of classification, admissibility of ITC, liability to register etc.; Authority for Advance Ruling (AAR) and Appellate Authority (AAAR). Anti-profiteering (s.171): benefit of reduced tax must be passed on; National Anti-Profiteering Authority wound up in 2022; now Competition Commission of India handles cases. Transitional provisions; migration. Tax recovery by banks etc.

Other taxes quick view: Central Excise Act 1944 - now only on tobacco products and petroleum (as residual); Customs Act 1962 (see T6); Compensation Cess phased out; State VAT on petroleum and alcohol; Professional tax; Stamp duty (State laws and Indian Stamp Act 1899); Securities Transaction Tax; Equalisation levy (the 6% on online advertisements was abolished from 1 April 2025 [VERIFY]); Gifts and Wealth tax (abolished). Digital Services Tax in international discussions.

key_provisions.content: Refund: within two years from the relevant date.
Demand and recovery - non-fraud/ fraud; unified s.74A from FY 2024-25.
Appeal to First Appellate Authority (3 months; 10% pre-deposit) / GSTAT (3 months; further 10%).
Offences and punishment: > Rs 5 crore - up to 5 years; non-bailable.
Power to arrest: only for specified offences.

landmark_cases.held: Upheld validity of ss.69, 132 and others but subjected arrest powers to Cr.P.C. safeguards, 'reasons to believe'; anticipatory bail available [VERIFY].

sections.title: Customs, Stamp Duty and Other Taxes
sections.articles: Customs Act 1962; Customs Tariff Act 1975; Indian Stamp Act 1899; STT; Black Money Act 2015
sections.overview: A short, scoring block: customs levy and valuation, appeals, stamp duty and the 2023 Constitution Bench on unstamped agreements.
must_know: Customs Act 1962: levy of duty on import into and export from India (s.12); duties - basic customs duty (BCD) under the Customs Tariff Act 1975, IGST on imports under s.3(7) of the Customs Tariff Act, Social Welfare Surcharge (10% of BCD), Agriculture Infrastructure and Development Cess (AIDC), anti-dumping duty, safeguard duty, countervailing duty; classification by the Harmonised System of Nomenclature (HSN); valuation (s.14) - transaction value as per the Customs Valuation (Determination of Value of Imported Goods) Rules 2007; bill of entry (s.46) and shipping bill (s.50); Customs Act empowers search, seizure and arrest (ss.100, 104), confiscation (s.111 - improperly imported goods; s.113 - export), penalties (ss.112, 114); demand (s.28 - within 2 years; 5 years in cases of fraud/ collusion), refund (s.27 - within one year); drawback (s.74-75); baggage rules.

Customs appeals: Commissioner (Appeals) under s.128 within 60 days; Customs, Excise and Service Tax Appellate Tribunal (CESTAT) under s.129A (within 3 months); High Court under s.130 (substantial question of law); Supreme Court. Customs Authority for Advance Rulings; Settlement Commission replaced by Interim Board.
Cases: Commissioner of Customs v. Dilip Kumar & Co. (2018 - exemption notifications interpreted strictly).

Stamp duty: duty on instruments (documents) - Indian Stamp Act 1899 (Central law applicable to bills of exchange, cheques, etc. under Entry 91 List I) and State Stamp Acts (Entry 63 List II); instrument not duly stamped is inadmissible in evidence (s.35) until duty and penalty are paid; registration (Registration Act 1908) is separate. N.N. Global Mercantile Pvt. Ltd. v. Indo Unique Flame Ltd. (2023, five judges) held that an unstamped arbitration agreement is void; the seven-judge Bench in In Re: Interplay between Arbitration Agreements under the Arbitration and Conciliation Act 1996 and the Indian Stamp Act 1899 (13 Dec 2023) overruled it: an unstamped or inadequately stamped instrument is inadmissible but not void; it is a curable defect and the Arbitral Tribunal decides on stamping (cross-ref Part 6 ADR).

Securities Transaction Tax (STT) under Chapter VII of the Finance (No.2) Act 2004; Commodities Transaction Tax; Banking Cash Transaction Tax (withdrawn). Professional tax by States (cap Rs 2,500 - Art 276); Property tax by municipalities (Entry 49 List II); Entertainment tax - subsumed in GST except local bodies; Motor vehicle tax (Entry 57 List II); Toll (Entry 59); Wealth tax and Estate duty abolished; gifts are taxed as income under s.56(2)(x); Equalisation Levy withdrawn; Digital taxation; Carbon tax debate.

Black Money Act 2015: 30% tax plus 90% penalty on undisclosed foreign income/assets; Benami Transactions (Prohibition) Act: Ganpati Dealcom (2022); Prevention of Money Laundering Act 2002: tax crimes as scheduled offences; Fugitive Economic Offenders Act 2018 (cross-ref Part 2 BNSS ss.84-86 proclaimed persons); Smuggling and COFEPOSA - detention; Customs offences: s.135 (evasion of duty or prohibitions) - imprisonment up to 7 years; Customs offences are cognizable (for fiscal offences above specified amount) and bailable depending on value.

Tax and constitutional limitations: Art 265; Art 14 (reasonable classification); Art 19(1)(g) (tax cannot be confiscatory); Art 20(1); Art 300A; Art 301-304 (compensatory taxes do not violate freedom of trade - Automobile Transport (Rajasthan) v. State of Rajasthan, 1962); Entry 54 List II; Art 286; Art 366(29A) (deemed sale - works contract); Union of India v. Bombay Tyre International (1983) (valuation).

latest_developments.topic: Four Labour Codes in force; Central Rules notified
latest_developments.summary: The Ministry of Labour and Employment brought the Code on Wages 2019, the Industrial Relations Code 2020, the Code on Social Security 2020 and the OSH Code 2020 into force on 21 November 2025, repealing 29 Central Acts. Central Rules under all four Codes were published in May 2026, after which compliance obligations began to bite; States are notifying their own rules in phases. Model Standing Orders were issued for the new regime. Trade unions have opposed the Codes and the legal validity of aspects (e.g., 300-worker thresholds) is contested in public debate [VERIFY pending challenges].
latest_developments.why_it_matters: High-probability 'which Act has been repealed / which threshold now applies' questions.
latest_developments.likely_question: How many Central labour laws were merged into four Codes? (29)

latest_developments.topic: State of U.P. v. Jai Bir Singh - meaning of 'industry'
latest_developments.summary: By 6:3 the Court held the reference maintainable and by 5:4 refined the Bangalore Water Supply 'triple test' without a clear overruling; the 1978 test continues to govern pending disputes under the repealed Industrial Disputes Act and the refined test is prospective; the decision does not automatically fix the meaning of 'industry' in s.2(p) of the IR Code. Commentators note no clear majority on the reformulation (about four judges backed the new test) [VERIFY].
latest_developments.why_it_matters: A current-affairs favourite: bench strength, year, the test, the effect on hospitals/educational institutions.
latest_developments.likely_question: Which 1978 case's 'triple test' was reconsidered in 2026? (Bangalore Water Supply)

latest_developments.summary: The new Act replaces the 1961 Act, introducing the 'Tax Year' and a leaner structure. The substance of the heads of income, residence, TDS, assessment and appeals is retained. The new tax regime remains default; basic exemption Rs 4 lakh and s.87A rebate for income up to Rs 12 lakh (FY 2025-26). Returns for FY 2025-26 (AY 2026-27) are filed under the 1961 Act; Tax Year 2026-27 is the first under the 2025 Act [VERIFY Finance Act 2026 changes].
latest_developments.why_it_matters: Statute replacement questions are common in AIBE.
latest_developments.likely_question: The Income-tax Act 2025 is effective from? (1 April 2026)
